subtopic: CONDOLENCES TO FAMILY OF LATE GILLES VILLENEUVE
subsubtopic: MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity, under the provisions of Standing Order 43.
On Saturday, May 8, the world was stunned at the report of the death of our fellow citizen, Gilles Villeneuve, the brilliant Formula One driver, who was killed in a fatal accident under the tragic circumstances we all know. Canadians idolized Gilles Villeneuve and eagerly followed his daring feats around the world. He always did his utmost in every race, and we applauded his every success. Gilles Villeneuve was a symbol of our native courage, and this showed in his spirit and his determination and desire to win. He was an inspiration and an example to all young people because of his sense of discipline and his passion for excellence.
It is a heavy loss for the people of the riding of Berthier-Maskinonge-Lanaudiere, and especially for his friends in Berthierville, where he was born and where he grew up. In Gilles Villeneuve, Canada has lost one of its foremost representatives, and one of whom all Canadians were proud.
On behalf of all Canadians and the people of the riding of Berthier-Maskinonge-Lanaudiere, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe, Gilles Villeneuve's uncle, and the hon. member for Don Valley West (Mr. Bosley):
That this House extend its most sincere condolences to Mrs. Johanne Villeneuve and her children, his parents, Mr. and Mrs. Seville Villeneuve and all their family and to all the people in Berthierville in their cruel loss following the death of Gilles Villeneuve.

In light of the fact that under the Prime Minister's reign one of the many disasters to have befallen this nation is the drastic decimation in size and effectiveness of the Canadian military, and in light of the fact that his maritime venture provided visible evidence that he is "at sea", something we have always known as we have watched his repeated failures to pilot the ship of state, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart):

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, we were all shocked to learn on Saturday about the death of the Canadian Gilles Villeneuve in a terrible and unfortunate accident which occurred during his last lap around the Zolder circuit in Belgium. The Berthierville pilot had astounded the whole world by his ability, his spirit and his determination in an exclusive and increasingly dangerous profession. Even though quite young, Gilles Villeneuve had already won many Grand Prix and he had quickly won not only the admiration, but also the affection of all those who saw him in action in international races. He inspired and nurtured an exceptional pride among his fellow citizens. Canada and the rest of the world have lost a great champion.

Our auto racing star was only 32 years old. Numerous press reports claim that many of his own competitors would recognize that he was the best racer in the world. As a Canadian, I like and I am proud to believe them. But, over all, Gilles Villeneuve was a fighter, and his success was well-earned. Cherished by crowds everywhere in the world, he always remained a plain, simple man. Gilles Villeneuve was certainly one of the most likeable international athletes, and we are all shocked by his sudden death.

I want to express on behalf of the Canadian government our sincere condolences to his wife, his two children and his entire family.

subsubtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of National Defence. The Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence unanimously supported the report on the Armed Forces reserves which called for increases in personnel and updated equipment. The minister stated, "Most of the recommendations are realistic and some are already in the process of being implemented." Will the minister explain how the recommendations will be implemented when the Armed Forces reserves are being subjected to a 10 per cent cut in training funds, not including the inflation factor?

speakeroldname: Hon. J. Gilles Lamontagne (Minister of National Defence):
subsubtopic: IMPLEMENTATION OF COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS
speechtext: Madam Speaker, I would be surprised if the figure mentioned by the hon. member, a 10 per cent cut in the reserves, is correct. On the contrary, the reserve budget this year has been increased, if I am not mistaken, by about 15 per cent. In addition, we are trying to integrate more and more of our reserves with our regular operations so that it will be much more interesting for those in the reserves. It is more useful for the reserves to train with the regular forces. Therefore, I would say that we are attaching more and more importance to the recommendations of the committee. We have said the recommendation was realistic, and that it would be something that I, as Minister of National Defence, would like to implement as quickly as possible. However, we have to take the economic situation into consideration. With a 19.2 per cent increase in the budget this year, we are trying to give priority to reequipping the Armed Forces to address some of the earlier questions directed to me regarding the army, navy, and air force. With this increase in the defence budget, we are trying to give a fair share to the reserves.

Madam Speaker, I hope the minister's answer is not hypocritical, because the subcommittee and the minister have consistently been stating and recommending the importance of the reserves and their overall place in Canadian defence strategy. The information I have from many C.Os. in the reserves is that they have been orally advised of cuts. Which policy is the minister pursuing? Is he pursuing the recommendation of the committee that reserves should be increased to whatever size is necessary to respond to the mobilization requirements, or is he saying that their training funds will be cut, which will obviously decrease the number of men and women in the reserves? Which is it- increase or cuts?

subsubtopic: VOTING RIGHTS OF MILITARY PERSONNEL SPOUSES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is to the President of the Privy Council. In other words, for voting purposes she is only regarded as an extension of her husband. Is the minister taking steps to correct this anachronism by proposing legislation that would allow the wives of military personnel and of public servants serving overseas to designate the constituencies in which they will vote based on their own past residence in Canada?

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: VOTING RIGHTS OF MILITARY PERSONNEL SPOUSES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, as we know, the Chief Electoral Officer will be tabling his report at the beginning of the next session. speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have just been told that the hon. member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (Mr. Joyal), who was to rise at this point to pay tribute to Senator Harry Hays, whose funeral will be held today, as you know, will not be here to perform that duty. So I rise to fill in for him, because, among other reasons,
I sat in Cabinet with Mr. Hays during the years 1965-66.
As everyone knows, Senator Hays had quite a remarkable career both as a politician and a businessman. As a politician, he was mayor of Calgary for three or four years before being elected to this House where he sat from 1963 to 1966, if I remember correctly, as member for Calgary South and minister of agriculture. In 1966, he was elevated to the Senate.
In business as in politics, Senator Hays-

He showed great qualities of originality, of boldness, of inventiveness, as a cattleman in particular. He will remain a legendary figure in the development of that industry in Canada.
Besides these qualities which he had in great abundance, he had a lovely sense of humour. Just on the spur of the moment I can remember two of his interesting remarks. One day in this House, he coined the phrase, which is probably in Colombo today, "Statistics are for losers." On another occasion he said, "The greatest form of culture is agriculture."

subtopic: THE LATE HONOURABLE SENATOR HARRY HAYS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

This good humour was part of his trademark. For all the many services that he rendered to his country, we want to praise him today. As we all know, the most recent service he rendered was that of being co-chairman of the House of Commons and Senate Special Joint Committee on the Constitution with the hon. member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve (Mr. Joyal). I am sure the hon. member for Hochelaga-Maisonneuve regrets not being here today to pay homage to the late Senator Hays.
To the senator's family, to the people of Calgary and to the people of Alberta in particular, we express our deep regrets.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: THE LATE HONOURABLE SENATOR HARRY HAYS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I very much appreciate the action of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) in giving the House of Commons the opportunity to pay homage to the memory of the late Harry Hays. I do so in several capacities-as an Albertan, as Leader of the Opposition and as someone who had the honour of being a friend of the Hays family and the senator for at least the last 20 years. In fact, for a period of time he was a constituent of mine. One of his services, which we can perhaps attribute to his sense of humour, was that he always voted in the city of Calgary rather than at his ranch in my constituency. That was certainly something I appreciated.
He was, as the Minister of Transport said, a man not only of great good humour but also highly innovative. He was a man of boldness and of broad vision. That boldness and broad vision showed through in the many activities in which he not only engaged but excelled. Those of us in Alberta knew him as a rancher. He was not an ordinary rancher, but one of the few in the history of our country who actually developed a new beef breed, the Hays converter, which was developed on his ranch west of High River.
May 10, 1982

He was a very successful mayor of the city of Calgary at an important time in the life of the city. He was an aggressive and successful businessman. He was respected on all sides of this House of Commons and he served vigorously in the Senate. Throughout his life he was a highly innovative man, a man who was prepared to break new ground and who had the courage to follow the paths that he opened.
Certainly on behalf of myself and my colleagues here I want to express our appreciation to his wife Muriel, to his son Dan and to his grandchildren for the service that he gave to his province, to his country and to his industry. He is a man who stood tall in a region where standing tall is admired. He stood tall and cast a shadow, I believe, that was admired right across the country. We will all miss him.

subtopic: THE LATE HONOURABLE SENATOR HARRY HAYS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: THE LATE HONOURABLE SENATOR HARRY HAYS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I rise to speak on behalf of my party to express condolences to members of Senator Hays' family. His family has long been linked with agriculture in this country, especially with dairying, with auctioneering and with the livestock business. As was pointed out by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), Senator Hays was one of the few people in the history of our country to have actually succeeded in developing a new breed of livestock. He was active in both the east and the west. He developed his farm in the Calgary area. He watched the city of Calgary grow. He was part of that development as mayor and became physically part of the city, I suppose, because his home farm was largely taken over by that city.
He served as Minister of Agriculture. He moved to the Senate where he pursued the very important question of how farmers could achieve adequate returns from marketing livestock. He was very active as chairman of the Senate committee on agriculture. He was also actively involved as cochairman of the Special Joint Committee on the Constitution.
Senator Hays was a powerful, hard-working and sincere man. He will be missed by members of this House, by members of the Senate and in farm circles right across the country.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: THE LATE HONOURABLE SENATOR HARRY HAYS

May 10, 1982
Canada Elections Act
The House resumed from Friday, April 30, consideration of Bill C-58, to amend the Canada Elections Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I would like to continue the remarks I initiated on third reading of Bill C-58 when I was so unceremoniously cut off by the clock after a minute or two.
The President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) stated on that day that Bill C-58, which we are discussing, is almost identical to Bill C-21 which was tabled by the Progressive Conservative government on November 5, 1979. With the compromise worked out in committee which would see the election period run for 50 days as opposed to 47 days, as Bill C-58 originally intended, the President of the Privy Council is quite correct. However, he failed to mention on April 30 that the shortening of the election period is merely an isolated amendment to the Canada Elections Act and that when we introduced Bill C-21 it was within the wider spectrum of parliamentary reform, which I might add hon. members opposite have sadly neglected.
The bankruptcy of the party governing the country has been made especially evident by the events of this session. There has been considerable discussion and controversy in past weeks on the subject of omnibus bills. We witnessed some two months ago the reckless attempt of government to roll many different bills into one piece of legislation. The people of Canada know what happened to the government on that one.
Today we are witnessing a further example of government incompetence. It has before the House Bill C-58 to amend the Canada Elections Act, with specific reference to the length of the election period. The government is focusing the attention of the House on one isolated provision of the Canada Elections Act, when in fact the utilization of an omnibus bill to amend other just as important provisions of the Canada Elections Act would be highly desirable.
I am referring specifically to the statutory reports of the Chief Electoral Officer and his recommendation concerning required amendments to the Canada Elections Act. The recommendations of the Chief Electoral Officer have been sorely neglected by the present government. Why did the government not incorporate into Bill C-58 other recommendations which should be receiving the attention of the House today? Why are we not debating other amendments? Also we should be looking at the deletion of the present provision in the act concerning the posting of preliminary lists of electors. In my South Shore riding in Nova Scotia, the practice of posting in a public place a preliminary list of electors is causing great
concern, especially to those people living alone who risk the consequence of public disclosures of their name, sex, occupation, marital status and address.
In addition, today in the House I say that we should be looking at recommendations concerning third party advertising in an election campaign, the sale of alcoholic beverages on election day, the identification of printers and publishers on printed campaign advertisements, and a host of other recommendations too numerous to mention.
If the President of the Privy Council would like the detail of those amendments to the Canada Elections Act which we should be debating in concert with shortening the election period, I refer him to the 1974, 1979 and 1980 statutory reports of the Chief Electoral Officer which he apparently received but chose to ignore totally. The spirit within which we introduced Bill C-21 encompassed the reform of this institution which, in my 25 years as a sitting member, I can honestly say is desperately needed.
In 1979 we intended to introduce reform in keeping with the basic principles of parliamentary government but would have also seen the House become a more agressive representative body of the Canadian people. I do not believe that the House by itself should govern. However, I strongly assert that it should be able to check and balance those who do. If the House of Commons exists to represent the people of Canada and to legitimize the rule of the executive, it must receive the necessary tools to pursue that type of mandate.
I think it is imperative to note that although we have all heard the rhetoric of hon. members opposite, we have not yet seen any proposals for parliamentary reform come forward. Specifically, since 1980 we have not seen proposals which would govern the length of sessions, proposals which would fix the date for recesses, proposals which would hold ministers accountable for their actions in previous portfolios if those ministers were the only ones who could address the issues in question, or proposals which would more adequately allow time for private members' bills and motions. Most seriously, we have not seen proposals which would bring before the House debate on the current system of redistribution.
The Chief Statistician has released the 1981 census figures to the Chief Electoral Officer and the clock has started on the redistribution process. According to the calculations completed by the Chief Electoral Officer, the total number of seats in the House of Commons will increase from 282 to 310. These new seats will take effect in any federal election after October, 1984. The province of Ontario is to receive ten new seats; Quebec, four new seats; Manitoba, one new seat; British Columbia, five seats; Alberta, six seats; Newfoundland, one seat; and my native province of Nova Scotia will also receive one seat under the system.
Under the current system of redistribution, the government is quite content to let the House distend, inflate, and be bloated into what I call an unmanageable monstrosity. This is what will happen here. The origin of the redistribution system, the amalgam method, bears some investigation and comment.
May 10, 1982

The Representation Act, 1974, fathered by none other than the present Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen), came into force following the redistribution of 1971. This act was a temporary stop-gap measure which would among other things secure the seat of the hon. member for Cape Breton High-lands-Canso, if it did nothing else. A specific provision of the Representation Act, 1974, recognizing its temporary status, required the House subsequently to review the formula for setting the number of new seats and for distributing them among the provinces.
In 1979 the Progressive Conservative government intended to follow up this review. A detailed discussion paper had been prepared to deal with the question of restraining the number of federal representatives. However, following 1980, the present government has not yet had the courage to continue with that particular investigation. I say that with some sadness. Instead, we are left with a representative scheme which I submit will cost Canadian taxpayers an untold number of dollars and will make a mockery of this institution. Not surprisingly, the government intends to solve the problems associated with a burgeoning House of Commons through negligence. But I should like to tell the House today exactly what hon. members opposite are ignoring and to outline the potential for catastrophe if the representative scheme is allowed to run roughshod over the House and the country.
In less than 20 years the Canadian electorate can expect the House to expand to the ludicrous number of 375 members. In 1979 it was estimated that every member in the House incurs a cost to taxpayers of $140,000 in personal and staff salaries. My calculations indicate that these 93 new members in 2001 will result in a taxpayer expenditure based conservatively upon 1979 estimates of a minimum of over $13 million. This is for new members only. If we add that $13 million to the cost of the existing 282 members, it will be a figure of $53 million, all to be borne by the taxpayers of the country.
We must ask ourselves whether indeed there is a need for any more new members. That is the real question. Quite frankly, I concur with the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers) who is in his seat. He stated that the membership of the House should be frozen at its present 282 total. Canada is already one of the most overgoverned countries in the world.
I think it should be pointed out to those who claim that we should increase our membership because countries like Britain have a larger House than we do that Canada is governed under a federal system. Not only do our taxpayers financially support federal representatives; provincial legislatures also exist and those provincial members must be paid out of the public purse as well.
Perhaps it bears repeating to hon. members opposite that Canada has hit an economic decline. If they are not aware of that, I will repeat that Canada has hit an economic decline. To my memory, it is the worst that this country has seen in the past 40 years.
Canada Elections Act
1 say to the House that we do not need more members. What we do need, however, is more members who are willing to work harder. We who sit in this chamber are the elected representatives of the people. We have their trust and I submit that we should be here to set an example so that when hard times hit we are not insulated from the economic woes that are facing this country.
In the years that I have been in Ottawa I have come to believe that this is probably the most insulated city in Canada and I would go so far as to say it is the most insulated city in the entire world. Wherever you turn here, everything seems to be subsidized. For example, the National Arts Centre was built at a cost exceeding $50 million and apparently could not keep its door open without a federal subsidy. It received $10 million in 1980 and I note in this year's estimates that it will receive a subsidy of $15,797 million, almost $16 million just to see the show when there are people in this nation who will not even see the building. This subsidy is mainly for the benefit of the comfortable, insulated bureaucrats who live here in Ottawa.
The CBC is an example of another comfortable group. In 1980 the CBC was subsidized to the approximate amount of $579 million. When I look in the estimates books for this year I see a subsidy of $737,396 million. That is over $14 million a week. When I first came to Ottawa I remember speaking out about the CBC subsidy, which at that time was $52 million a year. I bitterly complained that $1 million a week was too much. It has now risen to $14 million a week in that brief period of time.
Where will it all end? When I quote figures such as those 1 must ask what the government is doing to set an example which would indicate that it is willing to face up to economic realities. Although this principle of calling for restraint by every Canadian is a noble one, it is a one-way street for those sitting on the government side of the House. It is a one-way street for cabinet who can, without flinching, earmark and approve the purchase of Petrofina at a cost estimated at between $365 million and $486 million more than was necessary to purchase it. But what did the government purchase? It acquired a chain of gas stations in eastern Canada. Did this make one more gallon of gasoline available to Canadians? I submit that we did not even get an ounce. Canadians will be paying dearly for at least the next 20 years for the blunder which was made by this government on that one transaction.
When my constituents write to me to ask, "Where is the money going? Why am I being taxed into bankruptcy?", I want them to know at least some of the reasons by illustrating them in my speech today.
This government has a perverted sense of equity which, I might add, is in keeping with its shoddy record of economic management. It is willing to spend over $250 million this year on self-serving advertising and publications in order to shore up its own image, while at the same time letting small businessmen and the home owners of this country go broke.

May 10, 1982
Canada Elections Act
More dangerous still, I submit, is the destruction of moral values, the breakdown of the home and the sense of frustration, hopelessness and despair faced by 1 'A million Canadians who are presently unemployed. This government is obviously ready recklessly to allow this House to expand in numbers which will curtail the ability of this House to be an effective voice of the people and will at the same time incur a greater cost to Canadian taxpayers.
I repeat again that we are here not only to represent our electors but to set an example for those we represent as the elected representatives of this country. We must all realize that there is a burden to be carried and if it means that we and our successors must represent a larger constituency, I say to you, Mr. Speaker, so be it. Not one of us should refuse to carry a heavier workload. We should be making a contribution to lessen the expenditures made to this government by the taxpayers.
This government forgets that it is not spending its own money, because it has none. I wish that the executive members of the government would remember that the government has no money and it is spending the taxpayers' money which is given to it in trust and in the hope that it will spend it wisely.
There are young, middle-aged and senior Canadians who are hurting today because of mismanagement by the present administration. If the burden imposed on them by this government can be lessened by not increasing the number of members in the House, I submit that that should be done. It can only be done by the executive and other members on that side of the House who support this government. It can only be done if they agree that this bill should be withdrawn.
Through the withdrawal of this bill, the government would indicate that it is not speaking pure rhetoric when it addresses the House or calls for restraint. It would indicate that it is at least making one move in good faith. It would be a gesture which would save millions of taxpayers' dollars and in the long run prevent further difficulties for members who represent the Canadian people. Members would have an adequate opportunity to represent their electors in the House.
The removal of this bill would be a good decision. Already members on the opposition side of the House have difficulty in making the needs of our people known in the chamber. Today, for example, one just has to see how many opposition members were recognized in the question period. I am not condemning anyone because the Speaker does her best, but if the size of the House is increased as proposed by this bill, there will be even less opportunity to present the views, needs and aspirations of the people we represent. It will be more difficult to speak in the chamber. It is for those reasons, and for many others I could give if time permitted, that this bill should be withdrawn.
Members on the other side of the House should be prepared to work harder and for a larger constituency. We on this side are prepared to follow that course. The sooner hon. members opposite come to their senses and take some responsibility of the state of the House of Commons and the state of this country, the better it will be for all Canadians.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very happy to take part in this debate at the third reading stage of Bill C-58. Before I commence, I would like to make one or two comments on the remarks just made by the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse).
While I do appreciate his concern that the membership of this chamber will get bigger and bigger according to some ancient formula that was agreed to many years ago, indeed generations ago, I would also like to remind the hon. member that we have somewhat of a dilemma on our hands. If we do not expand the number of members in this House, it therefore means that our constituencies will get larger and larger. I have nothing against larger constituencies personally; I have a very small constituency geographically, although in terms of population I have one of the larger ones in the country.
Does the hon. member for South Shore fully appreciate what this could conceivably lead to? It could lead to a situation, not one which obtains in the United Kingdom but which obtains south of our own border in the United States, where the average electoral district at the House of Representatives level comprises about a quarter of a million voters. Consequently, congressmen to whom I have spoken constantly lament the fact that they can never get to know their constituents. They each represent anywhere from a quarter of a million to half a million people at the House level in the United States. That is the average.
Apart from the fact that it costs maybe half a million dollars or a million dollars to get re-elected through their electoral system, they then must make their presence felt in their electoral districts through a whole army of assistants who are financed by the taxpayers. The minimum number of assistants in the constituency or electoral district of one congressman in the United States is 14. I believe most of us have only one. Some of us may have two part-time or three part-time assistants, depending on the nature of our ridings. Does the hon. member for South Shore suggest that by keeping the numbers down in this chamber, some day we will have 10, 12 or 15 assistants in the constituency in order to help us with our work there? I see that he is shaking his head in the negative. I did not think that was what he meant.
Also, congressmen in the U.S. each have at least a minimum of eight assistants in their Washington offices. I am quite sure we do not want to reach that level here. However, I started out by saying that it was a dilemma. It is a dilemma because I personally do not want to see this chamber getting any bigger than it is. In fact, I like the British House. I like Westminster where there is a very small chamber, debate is kept at a very intimate level, and only those members who are directly involved in a debate sit in the chamber at that time. The debates at Westminster are very informal. They are very exciting at times. It is not a huge chamber; it is an intimate area in which to debate. It was that great Tory, Winston Churchill, who argued, after the bombing of the House of Commons in London in World War II, that we should not
May 10, 1982

build a new, bigger one, but rather we should build a new one which was in fact smaller than the previous one in order to retain that intimacy. 1 do not think distribution or redistribution is even considered in this bill and I do not know why we have gone off on this tangent. However, I thought I would very briefly respond to the hon. member for South Shore.
There are four basic compromises or agreements in Bill C-58. Therefore, 1 doubt very much whether we will protract this debate much longer this afternoon. First, it makes the minimum period of time for an election 50 days. We have been accustomed to minimum election periods of 60, 62 or 65 days which, in modern times, is far too long. With the electronic media that we have at our disposal today, with jet planes which can jet leaders from one end of the country to the other in a matter of four or five hours, it is nonsense to say that a minimum election period must be 60 days.
The original draft of the bill stated that we would have a minimum period of 47 days. Some of us felt that that was far too short, so the steering committee and the committee itself arrived at a compromise whereby elections would be a minimum of 50 days.
Another aspect of Bill C-58 which is worthy of note is that nomination day will now be uniform and it will be "E" day minus 28, or 28 days before election day. This gave the committee some concern. We heard representations from a few hon. members who represent very large geographic areas of the country. Their ridings are very large and they have what I think they call mobile nomination meetings, or travelling shows, as I believe someone referred to them. There is some legitimate concern in very large areas of the country, very large ridings, where a series of nomination meetings are held and there may be three or four days between each meeting.
However, the committee did agree that 28 days should be long enough because what we should keep in mind is that what we are discussing here is not a limit of 28 days. That is the minimum period. Any constituency organization of any party worth its salt will get its incumbent member renominated well before 28 days prior to an election, and those which do not have incumbent members are not worth their salt unless they, too, hold nomination meetings well in advance of the election call. Consequently, there is no law prohibiting a political party from nominating a candidate months in advance or, indeed, even years in advance of an election. I see no problem there unless the incumbent member should decide at the last moment not to run again in one of those very large geographic electoral districts, or the incumbent member or the nominated candidate in that campaign takes seriously ill and cannot run and must withdraw at the last moment or, most sadly of all, if the candidate or the incumbent member should die, which would mean that a nomination meeting would have to be immediately organized. That is one consideration which still bothers me and I know it bothers some other hon. members as well. Nonetheless, the committee has agreed to let the 28 day minimum period go by.
Another good aspect of Bill C-58 is that it extends the voting period at the electoral officer's office from two weeks to
Canada Elections Act
three weeks for those who will be away on election day, excluding, of course, those days on which an advance poll will be held. Therefore, it gives the voters an extra week in which to vote at the returning officer's office. We are in agreement with that aspect.
A fourth aspect of Bill C-58 is that it extends the enumeration period from four days to seven days, and 1 think that is certainly a positive move. It also allows for at least one enumeration day to be on a weekend, preferably, I think, the Saturday of the two days, or it could be Sunday, I am not quite sure. In the past, we have found that in big urban areas, even in certain sections of a riding like mine, particularly where there are many apartment buildings, couples work during the week and this provision will allow the enumerators to get around and see them on a Saturday morning, or even on a Saturday evening.
While I am referring to enumerations, I must say that I am still concerned at the sloppiness of enumeration in this country.
I am not pointing my finger at any one person or office with regard to sloppiness. I mentioned it in committee. I am not satisfied that all the people who are eligible to vote get on the voters' list; I think we all know they do not. I am not satisfied that all those who are not allowed to be on the voters' list are, indeed, excluded from the voters' list. I do not know how to toughen up enumeration. I certainly do not want to see enumerators going into homes and demanding I.D.s, citizenship papers, proof of age and so on. That smacks too much of authoritarianism. Certainly, though, we will have to take a new look at enumeration to ensure that those who are eligible to vote are on the list and that those who are not eligible to vote are not on the list.
There are many other reforms much more important than Bill C-58 which should be brought on stream and put on the Order Paper just as soon as it is humanly possible. With all due respect, we have wasted two years in election reform which, I think, was a major issue in the 1980 election. It was certainly mentioned from one end of the country to the other. In two years all we have really come up with is Bill C-58. We have not touched upon redistribution. We have not touched upon enumeration. We have not touched upon mobile balloting for those who are physically incapable or find it physically difficult to get to the polls, yet the report of the special committee on the disabled brought that in as one of their foremost recommendations.
I know the parliamentary secretary has undertaken to ensure that such legislation will be forthcoming, but time is beginning to run out. If it will require the same kind of time frame to bring in these other reforms, redistribution and mobile balloting for the physically infirm as well as better enumeration laws and the whole question of time, with four and half different time zones in this country, how much longer will it take to bring in these much needed and more important reforms than the four mentioned in Bill C-58?

May 10, 1982
Canada Elections Act
We must impress upon the government that after the Chief Electoral Officer's report comes in on the eve of the next session, which I presume will be early next fall, that draft legislation should be put before the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections for our consideration so that these electoral reforms will be in place well in advance of the next election, which I anticipate will probably be two years from this spring, although a lot of Liberal backbenchers would prefer the spring of 1985 for obvious reasons that have nothing to do with election reform.

speechtext: You mean 1995.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
That would probably help them more, but it would not help the country.
There is an important point 1 would encourage the parliamentary secretary to bring to the attention of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Pinard) in drafting new legislation, and that is the whole question of polls during election campaigns. We had a debate in this House, in which I took part, on a private member's bill with respect to polls during election campaigns. I am opposed to them and think they should be done away with. People should be able to think for themselves during election campaigns. Polls are destructive and negative. They give supporters of all parties either a false sense of security or false direction on how to plan their election campaign.
These are some of the reforms I would like to see brought on stream by the government as quickly as possible. I mentioned the four main parts of Bill C-58. I sincerely hope that passing this bill today will indicate to the government the willingness of those on this side, and they will ensure that these other reforms are brought in as soon as the Chief Electoral Officer's report is given to the government early this fall.
With those remarks, I look forward to more creative work in the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections so that we can update our election laws and bring some of them at least into the 1980s.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is again a privilege to have the opportunity to bring to this House of Commons some of the thoughts I gathered over the several months preceding the redistribution process that we are now undertaking. I am disappointed that the government did not take this period of time to bring in the type of election reform mentioned by the two previous speakers. The government is really missing the boat by not doing something like that during this period. Both the spokesman for the government and the Chief Electoral Officer stated that they did not think the next election would be fought on the redistributed boundaries. This is why we are going through this exercise.
Surely we learned our lesson in the 1972-74 period and prior to the 1974 election. Suspension law was brought in and that election was fought on old boundaries. We are going to go through the same thing again in 1984, yet we are still putting people in the field. Orders have gone out, the law has to be abided by, the Chief Electoral Officer's hands are tied and he
cannot do anything about it. This is not only a useless exercise, but costly.
If the government had wanted to be responsible on this issue, it would have taken this period of time that apparently will be available and brought in some of these measures which are fundamental to the House of Commons. We do not need to make this House larger; 1 am sure there are ways and means of making it more effective. Increasing the membership in this House will not accomplish that.
I have always maintained that Canadians are the most overgoverned people in the world. We in Canada have over a thousand elected or appointed officials to govern 25 million people. The best example I can give is the United Kingdom which has 635 members for 57 million people.
I was pleased with the very good discussion we had in committee on my private member's bill, C-223. The witnesses who appeared before that committee represented a fairly broad spectrum of our society. We were told that unless we exercise some control in the immediate future, the whole thing will explode and there will be too many chiefs for the number of people we have. We have to look at this.
The current formula for reapportioning seats in the House of Commons is basically unrealistic. It does not take a great mathematician to figure out what the size of the House will be in 10, 20, 30, 40 or 50 years when every ten years the size of the House goes up by 10 per cent or more. This cumulative effect will be disastrous down the road. Now is the time to do something about it.
Canada is overgoverned compared with other countries in the world. We have at least three levels of government in every city, town, village and crossroads hamlet in this country. In some jurisdictions where there is a metro or regional form of government, there are four levels of government. In Ottawa there are five with the National Capital Commission, it being the non-elected fifth tier of government.
In most European states there is a pure federal or unity form of government. There are no levels in between the municipalities and the central government. If you look, Mr. Speaker, at the statistics in Europe-France, Britain, Germany and others-you will see there are far fewer lawmakers, far fewer legislators and far fewer politicians representing far more constituents, far more voters.
Increasing the size of the membership of the House of Commons will do little or nothing to bring about the reform of government which is so desperately needed in this country. It will serve only to dilute the powers and functions of members of Parliament. For years this country functioned with fewer than 250 Members of Parliament. The size was increased to 264 and then expanded to 282.
The present formula, a 1974 amendment to the British North America Act, has so far shown us that it is a cumbersome and unworkable piece of arithmetic. We know how long it takes to put the reapportionment in place. We know that as soon as it is in place, it is obsolete and redundant.
May 10, 1982

Redistribution is supposed to follow every ten-year census, but by the time the draftsmen and the bureaucrats have the new boundaries and numbers in place, they are outdated and do not have any built-in checks for areas of rapid growth. Certainly this is what is happening in my province. Under the present system, at any given time we are entitled to anywhere from three to five members more than we have, but we are willing to change that. As soon as a province experiencing a high growth rate has its seats reapportioned, it is almost immediately underrepresented and must wait another ten years before any alterations can take place. The 1981 census figures have only recently been available to the Chief Electoral Officer and, by law, he has to set the machinery in motion to redistribute electoral boundaries across Canada. On the basis of the experience of the 1970s, we can rest assured that the new boundaries will not be in place for the next federal election. They will be in place for the federal election we will have at the end of this decade; by that time they will again be outdated, and a year or two later the same process will begin anew.
Surely there is an argument for retaining the Elouse of Commons at its present size or for making it smaller. Common sense requires that. Economy demands it. Running Parliament is not a run-of-the-mill operation. It is an extensive business, and we have an obligation to set an example for the rest of the country.
My colleague, the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn), mentioned that if we followed the route the United States has taken, there would be more people working in our constituency offices. I do not think that is really necessary. If there was less government interference in private business and in our private lives, we would not have so many problems and it would not take so much time and so many people to make the system work.
Ours is an expensive business, and we have an obligation to set an example and run a lean, thrifty operation. Increasing the size of the membership of the House will place demands on the public purse. I fear that increasing the size of this House would reduce the role of the individual Member of Parliament to that of a mere cypher to be around only at voting time in the House. More and more power would be concentrated in the cabinet and in the office of the Prime Minister. There is too much power there now, and there are no checks on that power. That does not augur well for the common good.
The House of Commons is the highest court in the land. Its members should be close to the decision-making process and close to the framing of the laws which direct our society. In every instance members should be elected to this House directly by their peers. We do not need proportional representation. We need a representative body which mirrors our society, our culture and our Canadian way of life. If reform is needed, it is needed in the manner in which we function. If
Canada Elections Act
reform is needed, it is needed in the areas of rules and committees and in the frugal use of the time of the House. There are ways by which we could accomplish this, and it would be for the betterment of our society if we did.
Let me return to the matter of the Senate. The Senate is a prime candidate and ripe for reform. Senator Duff Roblin made an excellent speech on this very important topic in that chamber not too long ago. I wish the government would move in the direction suggested in our advice. It is the responsibility of the government to reform the Senate. That would make Parliament more relevant, more effective and more responsive. If changes to the Senate were made, I am sure that would free up Members of Parliament to accomplish much more.
We must realize that the Canadian people expect us to make major adjustments. Canadians do not want an increase in the membership of the House of Commons. Canadians want an elected Senate. They do not want political parties appointing people to the other place. They do not want provinces appointing the membership of the other place. They want a responsive membership in the Senate, and they want senators elected so that they, too, must return to the people and be responsible.
If we do not make some of these changes, 1 really do not know what will happen to our country. I know there is a great deal of unrest in my province. That unrest is the result of a government which will not accept its responsibility. It will not allow other people to change the system, but it will do nothing itself. It has a dog-in-the-manger attitude, and that is not acceptable to those of us in the House who are in opposition or to the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO SHORTEN PERIOD REQUIRED TO HOLD ELECTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I realize that the subject of electoral reform is not one which causes grown men to cry or women to swoon. However, how we handle an election in a parliamentary democracy is extremely important, and what takes place and the procedures utilized in an election make all the difference in the way democracy operates.
I have no objections to this bill. It comes to us from the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections. That committee of this House is one of the few which operates on an allparty basis. All its members have the same interest in making the system better. It is a pity there are not more committees working on that basis.
With respect to this bill, the Standing Committee on Privileges and Elections reached a consensus on two important figures. It was agreed that the length of election campaigns should be revised from the initially-intended 47 days up to 50 days and that the length of the enumeration period be increased from four days to seven days. I will be asked many questions about why 50 days and not 30 days or 20 days? I think the answer lies in the fact that there is a rural point of view and an urban point of view. For those of us coming from defined urban areas a much shorter election period would be quite satisfactory.
We can get around our ridings and meet the people by various means of communication. Because of this a much

May 10, 1982
Canada Elections Act
shorter election campaign would be appropriate, as is the case in many provinces. Elowever, one riding in the middle of British Columbia is 500 miles long. The hon. member for Athabasca (Mr. Shields) must attend a minimum of five nomination meetings in five different centres, all of them hundreds of miles apart. That makes a difference. The best compromise, and the one 1 think all parties agreed on, was that rather than 47 days, 50 days made a great deal of sense and seemed to be a reasonable compromise satisfactory to both the urban point of view and to the rural point of view.
The Canadian Chamber of Commerce stated recently that the current 60-day campaign was established prior to the development of modern transportation and electronic communications. At the last annual meeting of the chamber delegates agreed that a two-month interruption of public business for an election campaign was unnecessarily long and that shorter campaigns would benefit Canadians by concentrating debate, providing a better public focus on issues and policies, reducing the cost of a campaign and minimizing interruptions of the nation's business. As a result of this bill, 50 days will be a shorter period and, hopefully, will meet some of the demands and concerns of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce.
The duration of election campaigns varies from country to country. The institution of permanent voters' lists in Australia and the U.K. has made it possible for much shorter election campaigns. The Chief Electoral Officer of Canada has investigated the suggestion of a permanent voters' list for Canada. We do not have one, and I doubt very much whether, all things considered, we should. The estimated cost of a permanent voters' list for Canada is some $30 million per year. On a cost basis it seems that is one aspect of electoral reform which should not be undertaken in this country.
The enumeration period and the difficulties of enumeration are probably the chief problems encountered at the beginning of any election campaign. This is one reason we fought hard and that finally the committee again came to total agreement that the enumeration period should be lengthened slightly to ensure better enumeration, particularly when the weekend is available. As Bill C-58 now reads, it will guarantee a period of 11 days between the calling of an election and the beginning of an enumeration; five days for the candidates to select their enumerators and five and a half days for the returning officer to train them. The Chief Elector Officer is in favour of this as,
1 think, will be most members of the Elouse who have studied the issue.
There will be questions about the Provincial election periods in the different provinces. It is 21 days in Newfoundland; 26 days in P.E.I.; 36 days in New Brunswick; 32 days in Quebec; 37 days in Ontario; 35 days in Manitoba; 28 days in Saskatchewan; 29 days in Alberta and 38 days in British Columbia.
I point out to those who wish to compare the federal position with that of the provinces that a federal riding normally encompasses an area which may include as many as five provincial ridings and constituencies. On that basis alone a
federal campaign must take somewhat longer than a provincial campaign.
It is not what is in this bill that concerns me, Mr. Speaker, it is what is not in the bill. It is the fact that the government has overlooked so many things that should have been part of the legislation. I doubt if the debate would have gone as long today had the government brought in the reforms that should be in the bill. Other hon. members have spoken about these things, such as the number of representatives in the House and some thoughts about parliamentary reform and other recommendations made by the Chief Electoral Officer over the years about which nothing has been done. That is unfortunate, Mr. Speaker.
I should like to turn now to the question of new boundaries because the machinery for that is now in place. The Chief Electoral Officer says that he will not change the boundaries, will not add the 29 seats, and cannot have that work done prior to October, 1984. If the work cannot be done prior to 1984, that means it is extremely likely that the next federal election campaign will be fought on the same boundaries as exist today. If that happens it means considerable injustice in many ridings of the country. I will give a few examples, Mr. Speaker. Richmond-South Delta will have 55 per cent more population than other ridings; Surrey-White Rock-North Delta will have 65 per cent more than other ridings; Calgary East will have 88 per cent more than other ridings; and Pembina in Manitoba will have 67 per cent above quotient. There are several ridings in Ontario that are in an even worse situation.
If the representation order does not come into force before the next federal election, members from oversized constituencies will be overburdened for years to come. The present position is punitive and discriminatory so far as these members and their constituents are concerned.
Another matter was raised today in question period by the hon. member for Kingston and the Island (Miss MacDonald). The wives of servicemen are required to vote where the husband is registered. The problem with that is that that provision is not contained in the Canada Elections Act. Certainly those wives who are Canadian citizens should have the right to choose where they wish to vote and under what circumstances.
Many other recommendations were made by the Chief Electoral Officer which could have been included in the bill, such as deletion of the present provisions concerning the posting of preliminary lists of electors; more flexibility in setting the maximum member of electors per polling station; promoting or opposing the election of a party or candidate through media interviews; and partisan activity on polling days.
There have been representations from every tourist organization in the country about the sale of alcoholic beverages on polling day. This is an outdated provision still contained in the Canada Elections Act. It is costing us hundreds of thousands of dollars in a federal election period and is damaging the tourist industry. Surely a simple matter like that could have been corrected in this bill.
May 10, 1982

Another problem is third party advertising. The government does not know yet what it will do about that. The identification of printers and publishers on printed advertisements is another problem, as is the change in the names of electoral districts. There should be clarification of the discretionary powers of the Chief Electoral Officer as contained in subsection 13(8) of the Canada Elections Act.
I did not invent these things, Mr. Speaker; they are contained in reports of the Chief Electoral Officer made to Parliament in the past and no action has been taken on them. This makes his job much more difficult. In this case the government is not guilty of excess; it is guilty of not doing anything. The Chief Electoral Officer has made a good many recommendations that should have been looked after.
Another matter that should have been addressed in the bill is that of vacancies. There are three seats in the House of Commons which are vacant. After 60 days of a seat being declared vacant surely a date could be set for a byelection. The law as it stands is totally unfair to the people of three ridings who have no representation in this House. The government does not have to announce the date of a byelection prior to September and then it can be announced for any time up to and including February, 1985 or until this Parliament ends.
I should point out that the riding of Timiskaming has not had a sitting member since January 22, Broadview-Greenwood has not had a member since March 2 and Leeds-Grenville since the middle of March. It is now the middle of May, Mr. Speaker. When are these constituencies going to be represented in the House of Commons? Why is the government afraid to look after that problem?
1 am in favour of the bill as it stands, Mr. Speaker. It represents a compromise among the parties and will operate in the best interests of Canada. In my view, its main defect is that it addresses one small problem, rather than the hundreds of problems that exist.
I think we should let this bill go through, Mr. Speaker, but we should plead with the government to bring in the other reforms that are necessary as soon as possible. I am ready to vote, Mr. Speaker.

Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to speak on this bill today but I should like to take about three minutes to clarify points raised by hon. members opposite.
I am pleased that we appear to be at the end of the debate on the bill. Had we enforced the rule of relevancy, however, I think the debate would have been much shorter today. Most of the discussion that has gone on did not have anything to do with the bill but, being on who never likes to cut off debate, I thought it would be good to air the concerns that some hon. members have when the broader subject of elections is raised.
This bill does not deal with redistribution, Mr. Speaker. Some hon. members are concerned about redistribution, and in response to that the government agreed to refer the matter of
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
redistribution to the standing committee. As a result there have been a number of meetings on that subject, expert witnesses have been called and the issue has been aired.
This bill does not deal with redistribution, however; it deals with a shorter election period, reducing it from 60 days to 50 days. This is accomplished mainly by eliminating the need for the preliminary lists that are posted.
It also lengthens the enumeration period from four days to seven days so as to provide for a more thorough enumeration. All parties gave somewhat in the negotiations on this bill and I understand all parties have agreed to it. It is an improvement and moves in the right direction and I am delighted that it appears it will receive third reading today.

speakeroldname: Hon. Andre Ouellet (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF ASSISTANCE TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
that Bill C-109, to provide for payments to persons in respect of dwellings insulated with urea formaldehyde foam insulation, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am taking the floor to propose that the House approve this bill, which will enable us to provide for payments to owners of homes insulated with urea formaldehyde foam insulation. First of all, I should like to make it clear that notwithstanding the lack of comprehension of UFFI victims for our government assistance program and the lack of confidence in the government expressed, from time to time, by certain victims, and despite the accusations and insults addressed by some home owners to the government and to me in particular, the Canadian government is determined to find a solution to the problems besetting the owners of UFFI homes.
Personally, I do not harbour any resentment or bitterness with respect to those people who twice came to demonstrate in front of my constituency office. I think that their exasperation and their demands are the natural result of the suffering, anxiety and uncertainty they are experiencing. I want to make it clear to these people that I shall discharge fully my ministerial responsibilities-namely, to find a solution to this problem,-with all the necessary energy and conviction, and that we, as a government, must find a solution to their problems. I wish they would understand that my task would be much easier if I now had all the answers to their questions. It is easy for men and women in the public eye to take part in public rallies and tell UFFI victims what they want to hear. It is much harder to find a solution to their problems.

May 10, 1982
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
I am looking for a scientific answer, because I believe it is important to give UFFI victims sound advice. It would be easier, of course, to provide temporary solutions to the problem, instead of concentrating on the scientific approach to find out what can be done to reduce gas levels produced by UFFI. I cannot say that I am very happy about my lack of popularity, but I am prepared to put up with it, because I feel it is my duty to find a real solution to the UFFI problem. I also see it as my duty not to waste public funds, and that is why distinctions must be made and why there are profound differences of opinion about what the Government of Canada wants to do now to help UFFI victims and what the victims themselves would like to see done. The first distinction and issue on which there is a basic difference of opinion relates to removal of the product. Our assistance program is based on a series of measures aimed at reducing formaldehyde gas levels in homes. Our program clearly does not stress removal of UFFI.
And why not? It is because, to date, experts at the National Research Council of Canada have not told us that removal of UFFI should be a priority. On the contrary, all the scientific information available to us shows that UFFI removal in homes should be seen as a last resort, and that before contemplating this costly operation, there are many other approaches that should be tried by home owners. This is therefore a first and very basic difference of opinion. We feel that the tax-free grant of up to $5,000 is an adequate response to the needs of most people who will have to do work on their homes. On the other hand, UFFI victims who believe that the product must be removed right away, will feel that $5,000 is certainly not enough. This difference of opinion will continue as long as the scientific experts working for the National Research Council of Canada have not reached a conclusion. In fact, from the research that has been done, it seems that home owners who did remove the product from the walls of their homes were unable to treat satisfactorily the framework and woodwork, and there is a possibility that these parts of the house are still being affected by the gas and that as a result, only part of the problem has been solved. We must therefore wait for the findings of the experts before we decide whether or not the product should be removed from the walls of homes insulated with UFFI.
The other basic subject of disagreement concerns the health hazard represented by this product. We know that the officials of the department of National Health and Welfare have set a standard of 0.1 parts per million, and all the opinions we have obtained suggest that if the formaldehyde contents in a house is lower than this level of 0.1, there should not normally be any health hazard. Some owners with parents, children, or, in some case, adult relatives who have been affected by the product do not accept the standard of 0.1 and consider the product dangerous at an even lower level. Needless to say, this standard is the subject of many discussions and major contradictions. I must admit that I am not a scientist or a physician and
that therefore, regarding the implementation of this government program, I must rely not on the very legitimate impulses and reactions of the victims of this product, but rather on the opinion of experts and physicians; as long as the scientific and medical aspects of this issue have not been settled, we shall find it difficult to understand and interpret the program of the Canadian government.
Having said this, Mr. Speaker, there is one thing that I want to make clear. The government of Canada should not be blamed for this matter. I know that, later on in this debate, members opposite will attempt to throw the blame on the government or the officials acting on its behalf. That is simply partisan politics and I do not believe that it is to the advantage of those affected by this problem. I think that we must recognize one thing, namely that the government has attempted to develop a whole series of measures to provide generous assistance to those affected by this product. Bill C-109 now under consideration is in keeping with the initiatives taken by the government of Canada to help home owners now facing certain problems. The action we are taking will affect many areas, and I would like to summarize briefly what we have done already and what we want to do with the co-operation of the victims themselves.
We have three major objectives. First, to give back confidence in the value of homes insulated with urea formaldehyde foam; second, to reassure the public about the health hazard; and third, to provide immediate assistance and as soon as possible to those who have health or housing problems because of this product. One of the first initiatives taken by the government was to create a co-ordination and information centre on urea formaldehyde foam insulation. The centre served as focussing point for the government assistance program by providing advice and information to the thousands of homeowners concerned.
As I am speaking, Mr. Speaker, I can say that some 21,050 people are already registered with this center and have filled out the necessary forms to take advantage of the assistance program we are making available. The results obtained from our testing programs through an extensive sampling of Canadian homes as well as scientific data have served as a basis for the legislation we are introducing today. I remind the House that Canada is the first country in the world ever to ban urea formaldehyde foam insulation. We are therefore pioneers in this area of science and engineering. The centre has pooled the resources of various federal departments and agencies as well as of many private organizations. I should like to emphasize that several governments are inquiring of Canada as to the means of coping with this problem in their respective countries, because this product has been in use for about ten years in some thirty countries. I should like to return now to the three main objectives I mentioned earlier. First, to restore
May 10, 1982

confidence in the value of homes insulated with UFFI. And as recently as this afternoon, during the oral question period, the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) put the following question to me, and I quote:
Has the government considered any further compensation for the 80 per cent of people who will not qualify for compensation under the bill today who find their homes being depreciated in value, who find they cannot sell their homes and who find they are having difficulty getting conventional mortgages on their homes?

Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the sensationalism which has surrounded this issue is directly responsible for the depreciated value of those properties. If 80 per cent of home owners, and those are the figures provided by the member for St. John's East, have no health problem or any difficulty with that product and consequently are not eligible for our program, it means that the fear which is being instilled by some people about that product is grossly exaggerated and unjustified. Our polls clearly indicate-

speechtext: What does the U.S. government say?

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF ASSISTANCE TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: I will get to that in a few minutes if the hon. member will allow me to speak and finish my remarks. Some of you are responsible for the prices being lowered on these homes because of your irresponsibility-

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF ASSISTANCE TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext: You are irresponsible. That is the reason. [Translation]

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: PROVISION OF ASSISTANCE TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, those who want to interrupt me show their irresponsibility because unfortunately, we have greatly overrated the importance of the problem. It is serious for those who are living in a house where the level of formaldehyde is too high. It is serious for those who are physically affected by the product, but it is not a serious problem for those who are not affected by the product and in whose house the formaldehyde level is acceptable. Consequently the value of those properties should not decrease. It is only because the matter received bad publicity that the problem was blown out of proportion, with 80 per cent of home owners having suffered a loss of value and needing our help and our program to restore their property's fair value. What we intend to do is provide free tests in order to scientifically and adequately measure the level of formaldehyde, take appropriate steps to bring it to an acceptable level and, above all, issue a certificate that they have safe homes that are fit for occupancy. It is to the extent that we can carry out that program that we will restore the value such properly insulated homes, whose occupants are not affected by the product, should always have retained, but as far as the other homes are concerned, we intend to reduce significantly the level of formaldehyde when it is felt to be too high.
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
We take the time needed to put the program in place. Some might say our progress is too slow. Clearly, Mr. Speaker, we are progressing slowly. We do so because we do not want to take the risk of putting the victims in a difficult situation. It is our view that we should not only give those home owners free expert advice, but also provide a list of qualified contractors that are duly approved to do the necessary work. We are convinced that a major part of the problem stems from the fact that the work was improperly done originally by unqualified contractors who did poor insulation job and are directly responsible to a large extent for the problem those owners of foam-insulated homes are facing today.
Now, if we want to help those homeowners adequately, it is important that we protect them and ensure that qualified contractors do the work on their homes. It is worthwhile, in my opinion, taking a few weeks, as we are now doing, to qualify those contractors in order that they do not take advantage of the victims of foam-insulated homes.
It is my view that over and above that problem confronting the Canadian men and women who have foam-insulated homes is the whole question of the Canadian public's attitude to the problem and our obligation to reassure the public as far as health hazards are concerned. That is why we have spent thousands of dollars on exhaustive research and development to find new and better corrective measures, so that through long and short-term medical research we may be better equipped against that type of threat that can strike at any moment. I feel that the money we have offered to the various independent associations of UFFI homes in order to help them group together and get, not only from the Canadian government but also from their provincial and municipal governments, concerned attention, direct help and, above all, generous understanding is money well spent. The money we granted those independent home owners' associations will bear fruit, I trust, and will enable us, in co-operation with the representatives of the various victims organizations, to do even better in the interest of the harmed parties, the home owners. Finally, in closing, I should like to mention this: some would have us believe that much has been done in this regard in the United States, like the hon. member who has just interrupted me asking about what is being done in the United States. Let me tell you about it.

The Massachusetts repurchase program, the so-called buyback plan, has been highlighted as being important and generous and as the thing we should do in Canada. I want to note that the cost of the buy-back plan was to be borne exclusively by industry, not by government, and that the manufacturers or the installers were held responsible for remedial actions. Indeed, the federal government of Canada considered this policy or option before formulating the types of assistance

May 10, 1982
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
programs we gave to Canadians. We did not follow the American experience because we knew that the American program was not very generous and was certainly not one which would quickly pay dividends for home owners. Instead we retained our program which gave free testing, technical advice and financial assistance of up to $5,000 to home owners in Canada in an attempt to remedy their problems.
On January 29, 1982, the superior court of Massachusetts set aside the ban and the buy-back regulations as a result of a challenge by the industry. Therefore, home owners in Massachusetts today are faced with no assistance. Just recently consumer protection agencies voted four to one to ban UFFI nationally in the United States. This is not yet in effect but it is expected that it will be in effect some time this summer. Those who compare what we have done in Canada with what was done in the United States should keep in mind that we have been much faster and much more generous in Canada in trying to help the victims of UFFI.
Another aspect of this question is that some people try to pretend that the federal government has some responsibility because the product was accepted under CHIP. Let me say that in 1977 the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation accepted this product, along with close to 100 other types of insulation, as an eligible building material under the Canadian Home Insulation Program. This acceptance was based on a standard developed under the auspices of the Canadian General Standards Board. Such voluntary standards are written through the medium of standards committees and the consensus process. The committees are representative of relevant interests including producers, consumers and other users such as retailers, governments and educational institutions, as well as technical, professional and trade societies and research and testing organizations. In other words, there are many other people involved in the standards boards.
The acceptance of this product under the Canadian Home Insulation Program was conditional upon the observance of rigid standards in its installation. Unfortunately, it is evident now that some contractors did not respect these established standards and the Canadian General Standards Board had no legal power to enforce them. This is known by the opposition as well as by us.
While politicians on the other side conduct petty politics over this question, they are not rendering any service to the home owners who have problems today. Prior to November, 1979, only two complaints had been registered with this department concerning this product. By September of the following year, approximately 100 complaints had been received. Although only a handful of these were substantiated, Health and Welfare Canada set up an independent committee
of experts to inquire into the potential health effects which could arise from the use of this product. This committee recommended in its interim report of December, 1980, that the use of UFFI be discontinued. The product was then banned under the Hazardous Products Act.
[ Translation]
That is the sequence of events that led the government to ban the use of that product and act as no other government has done in any other country. Obviously, the government wants to help the victims of that product. It has done something concrete about it. First, it banned the product to stem the evil. Second, it pleaded the homeowners' case before the board of review that was set up under the Hazardous Products Act, which act allows the industry to appeal the decision of the government. In other words, the government submitted the case of the victims before the board of review. The legal advisers of my department are the ones who pleaded the case for keeping the ban on the use of that product in Canada before the board of review in the interest of the victims. My departmental officials are the ones who developed the assistance program; our government is the only one in Canada to pay a certain amount of money to the victims of this product to the extent of $5,000 that is not taxable. Those are the facts. I wish the other provinces, especially Ontario and the province of Quebec, where a considerable number of home owners suffered from the use of that product, had shown comparable generosity towards the victims and offered each home owner $5,000, the amount we are willing to offer them. I feel it behoves other levels of government to quit talking and start doing something concrete like offering specific amounts of money with a view to helping the victims make the necessary repairs to their homes. I can solemnly promise in this House, Mr. Speaker, that my department and our government will continue to work towards helping the victims of UFFI.
We are anxious to become acquainted with the findings of the review board over which we have no authority and which is acting as a quasi-judicial body. We hope, however, to receive its report shortly and that it will confirm that this product is dangerous and must continue to be considered as such; once this matter is settled once and for all, we can take the second step which, in my opinion, is very important. I have already indicated publicly on a number of occasions that if the federal government is ready to do its share, the provincial governments as well as the private sector should likewise be ready to do their part. As soon as I am satisfied, on the basis of the review board findings, that the product is deemed dangerous once and for all, something I expect and hope, I promise to make further representations and step up my efforts to convince the provincial governments and the private sector, especially the manufacturing industry, to do their part and help UFFI victims.
May 10, 1982
