The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Ouellet that Bill C-109, to provide for payments to persons in respect of dwellings insulated with urea formaldehyde foam insulation, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.

subsubtopic: PROVISION OF ASSISTANCE TO HOME OWNERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to lead off this debate for our side, not only on behalf of the official opposition but on behalf of 80,000 to 100,000 families across Canada. I intend to speak out on behalf of some 250,000 to 300,000 Canadians who have suffered, are now suffering and who will continue to suffer from the effects of urea formaldehyde foam insulation unless this government acts.
I ask you to picture, Mr. Speaker, anywhere from 80,000 to 100,000 heads of households sitting in this chamber. Since it is impossible to visualize that many people jamming into this House of Commons facility, picture an overflow crowd at Olympic Stadium in Montreal and the Canadian National Exhibition Stadium in Toronto combined. I am absolutely certain that the vast majority, if not all, of the home owners whose homes are contaminated with UFFI would say to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), who just finished introducing second reading of Bill C-109, in one loud voice from those two stadium precisely what I am about to tell him-that this bill is a pathetic joke. It is an insult to those seeking responsible government action to assist them in their plight. It is a pitifully small band-aid measure which cannot begin to cover either the health damage or economic hurt which has been caused by this government.
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
Make no mistake, this Liberal government has created a monster that will not go away, a monster which will not respond to the pop-gun approach by the federal government in this bill.
Based on the government's urging, Canadians acted to insulate their homes using a government approved substance, one of several forms of insulation-as the minister correctly pointed out, but one which the government itself manufactured-urea formaldehyde foam insulation. There is absolutely no question that home owners or tenants, nor I daresay this government, would not have recommended and used this product knowing what we now know about its actual and potentially disastrous effects on people's health. I will deal with this government's undeniable responsibility in this UFFI crisis in a few moments.
I would like first to serve notice on the minister and the government that we on this side of the House would like to see reasonably speedy passage of the bill through second reading so that it can move on to the appropriate standing committee. I say that we would like to be reasonable in expediting this bill, although I know there are several of my colleagues in the official opposition, as I am sure there are a number of hon. members on the government side of the House, who are receiving strenuous representations from their constituents and who will want to enter this debate. We do, however, have a major concern about this legislation, quite apart from its glaring inadequacies in terms of compensation for home owners. Even as it stands, it is merely a skeleton of a bill. It contains only nine classes and everything in the bill depends on regulations to be made by order in council. These regulations are the heart and soul of the bill. They will set out who will be eligible for remedial grants, what criteria will apply and what compensation will be available to those unfortunate Canadians who qualify.
Surely the minister does not expect us to give him a blank cheque for some $55 million when it comes to the health, safety and financial security of a quarter of a million or more Canadians. Therefore, we on this side want to see the government's proposed regulations before we consider passing this bill; otherwise, we are being asked to approve legislation which we and Canadian home owners with UFFI will not see. Unless we have the regulations before us, we will not be able to examine them before the committee and individuals and groups of home owners will justifiably remain skeptical about the government's commitments to a truly effective and equitable compensation program.
Knowing the type of regulations which have recently come into being by order in cabinet, the minister should not be too surprised by our skepticism and concern. I urge the minister to let the committee examine the draft regulations that he has in

May 10, 1982
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
mind. Indeed, we may even wish to include some of those regulations in the legislation.
There is a precedent for this situation. During the Clark administration in 1979, when we were in second reading stage of Bill C-25, the Transportation of Dangerous Goods Act, our government broke with precedent in order to table draft regulations. The minister's co-operation in this connection concerning this bill's regulations would be most helpful. We have some questions to ask and recommendations to make concerning this bill, but 1 will deal with them later in my remarks. Let me come to the area of responsibility.

Mr. Speaker, I maintain that the federal government itself was the cause of the problem for Canadian home owners, that the federal government itself promoted UFFI and later banned it as dangerous. It was the federal government that warned Canadian consumers about the physical symptoms related to UFFI. It was the federal government that established the nationwide review board which will confirm its conclusions on UFFI, and the federal government therefore has the immediate and full responsibility of getting the Canadian home owners out of trouble. If this means a public statement, if this means another blow to the building industry, if this means another expenditure to protect the health of this nation, very well.
The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) cannot blame the media, the provinces, the manufacturers and the installers, nor can he blame the official opposition. He can only blame the ignorance of his department and his government, as well as the carelessness and the conflicts of interest which have brought about one of the worst tragedies in Canadian history.

The UFFI mess is a classic case of one arm or several arms of government not knowing what the other arms are doing. There is abundant historical evidence to prove this, although the government has thus far declined to answer some of our questions to confirm the facts. Mr. Cliff Shirtliffe, a research officer with the National Research Council, appeared before the hazardous products board of review. The minister says he is impatient to receive the report of that board of review. I can tell hon. members that there are a good many thousands of Canadians and many of us on the opposition side who are equally impatient to see those results.
At that board of review hearing on August 14, 1981, Mr. Shirtliffe said that he recalled a meeting in 1974 with CMHC and industry representatives to explain whether or not the reported cases of allergic reaction to the foam could be true. Assurance was given by the industry people that they themselves were not affected. However, as far back as 1974 there was a request to the Department of National Health and Welfare to review the toxicity of the foam. Mr. Shirtliffe also stated at the time that the problem concerning the gas released from the foam is that little is known about the effects of longterm exposure to low levels of the toxic chemical. He noted,
back then, that the federal committee investigating insulation materials was particularly concerned over the potential dangers of long-term exposure of children and older people to the gas.
Then in August, 1978 Dr. Richard Viau, who was then acting head of the chemical and fire safety program of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and who is now, I understand, its director, warned in an interview with Jim Travers of Southam News that "people should think quite carefully before installing this product in their homes". He went on to say, "Formaldehyde is a very irritating chemical and exposure can lead to headaches, allergies and a whole gamut of other problems". He also acknowledged that complaints of irritation and nausea had been received by government officials and that the government was aware of earlier studies done in Europe, Scandinavia and the United States describing problems with urea-formaldehyde foam insulation. But even as his own senior official was issuing this warning, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs was sending out thank you notices to home owners with UFFI. I have in my hand a faded copy of one of them, and it reads:
On behalf of the Government of Canada, I wish to express my appreciation for your participation in the conserving of energy through the Canadian Home Insulation Program.
It was signed by the minister's own hand, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs.
Only after several states had banned the use of the material, long after most of the 80,000 to 100,000 home owners took the government's advice and installed UFFI, did the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) begin to get concerned. There was then a series of news releases. I will just read the gist or the opening paragraphs of each of these releases. On September 19, 1980, the first time we heard of government concern, the government stated:
"Increasing reports of health problems that have been linked to the use of urea formaldehyde foam insultation are of serious concern to my department", National Health and Welfare Minister Monique Begin stated today-
A primary concern with UFFI is the release of formaldehyde gas into living areas, both during installation and for several years afterward.
That was the government's warning in September of 1980. Then, in December, 1980 another news release stated:
Steps to institute a temporary ban on the use of urea formaldehyde foam insulation were announced today by Health and Welfare Minister Monique Begin and Consumer and Corporate Affairs Minister Andre Ouellet.. .The government's decision to act at this time flows from the committee's expressed "serious concerns regarding the health hazards posed by the presence of formaldehyde in homes insulated with UFFI".
That was the expert advisory committee which the government had set up to look into problems relating to UFFI. If I may correct a statement which the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs made earlier during his remarks, the expert advisory committee said it was not prepared to recommend any level of formaldehyde as being safe. Therefore, I am wondering whether the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs is now rejecting the basic advice which prompted the ban on the product.
May 10, 1982

The committee also stated that each individual will react differently to formaldehyde under different climactic conditions and under different methods of installation. The expert advisory committee stated that the level of 0.1 parts per million is not a definite level of danger; it is simply an arbitrary one picked out of the air. That level was used based on the law of averages in terms of the way it affected Canadians.
Finally, on April 23, 1981 the Minister of National Health and Welfare recommended that the ban on the use of the product, urea formaldehyde foam, be continued because of chronic exposure to formaldehyde from leakage of gas into the living space of homes over long periods of time.
We are discussing the product itself here, the urea formaldehyde foam insulation, which is unstable. That is what the expert advisory committee was talking about and that is what the board of review is investigating now, the safety or otherwise of the product.
If there was any incorrect installation or if there were any faulty licences distributed to manufacturers, that is a matter for the courts to decide. It is something on which the provinces could be pursued. The main thing we are looking at now is the foam itself which is causing Canadians headaches and heartaches. It is the product I am concerned about here.
That is a little of the painful chronology which makes us realize how deeply the federal government became involved in this UFFI crisis as far back as 1974. Here we are in the second week of May, 1982 and we are actually getting a chance to debate second reading of a program the minister first announced on December 23, 1981. It was fully four and a half months before the government could get some legislation before the House and four and a half years after the government started to utter warnings to itself about the instability of this foam product.
Then the government delivers this mouse of a piece of legislation which is somehow supposed to redress the grievances of several hundred thousand Canadians who became unwitting victims of this government's blundering into one of the most monumental gaffs in Canadian history.
What has the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs been telling Canadians in the meantime? What encouragement does this umbrella ministerial spokesman for some five or six different government departments offer UFFI home owners? I do not know if the minister remembers a headline from Rock Forest in Quebec.

"Go and see a doctor if you are ill." The minister then added: "People should not wait for the government to act. If they have problems with their installation because it does not work as expected, they should sue the contractor or the manufacturer. If they have health problems, they should see a doctor."
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act

In effect, the minister tells them not to wait for the government to act if they are worried about the foam, that they should take it out themselves. A few minutes ago the minister told the House that the evidence he has from the National Research Council is that it would make the problem worse if they took it out, or to take it out only as a last resort. Small wonder Canadians are very confused and angered by this urea formaldehyde foam crisis.
In answer to questions my colleagues and I put to the minister in the House of Commons, and again just a few moments ago, the minister has been quick to blame everybody else in sight for this disaster. He blames the provinces, the contractors and the installers.

The government also has the impression that there has been an excessive amount of bad publicity and very often too little action concerning the UFFI and that we, of the Official Opposition, should help to appease the fears of the building industry about this crisis.

The fact remains that people are hurting. They know who is to blame. They were counting on government legislation to help them out of a mess that the government created. What did they get? They got Bill C-109, a remedial measure blanketed in a lot of comforting verbiage which does not come to grips with the real problem UFFI victims face. Stated simply, it is how they can make their homes safe and saleable, and is the government going to help them? This corrective measure, as the minister calls it, is too little and, for many Canadians with foam in their homes, already much too late.
That is not just my view as the official opposition critic for consumer and corporate affairs. I would hate to be politically partisan all the time on this issue, so 1 will call on an editorial in the Ottawa Citizen of Monday, April 12, 1982, entitled "Government offer not adequate". The Citizen is not exactly known for its hostility toward this Liberal administration, to put it mildly. I draw the minister's attention to the last three paragraphs of this government's most sympathetic newspaper:
The federal government will only offer up to $5,000 in grants for home owners suffering from foam fumes. And that maximum grant falls far short of the cost of removing the foam. Rather it will only cover cosmetic repairs to seal fumes from the foam inside the walls.
Prospective home purchasers don't care whether the foam is sealed or unsealed.
As Murray Coolican, Ottawa spokesman for home owners with foam, points out, the federal government's compensation plan is "too little, too late". Ouellet is duty-bound to provide compensation to deal with the problem his government helped create.
To lend some balance to this criticism that I have of the government's treatment of UFFI home owners, I will quote very briefly from three colleagues on the government side of the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. The hon. member for London West (Mr. Burghardt) has been receiving his share of flak from southern and western Ontario on this foam issue. I know because I recently attended a meeting in

May 10, 1982
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
London of 350 home owners who brought their legitimate concerns in a very forceful manner to that hon. member and myself. The hon. member for London West at the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs said it for all of us when he told the minister:
The thing that concerns me, though, and I am sure it concerns all of us, Mr. Minister, is this fear of the unknown. Many people today are experiencing health problems; there is no doubt about that. Whether they have evidence from their doctors or not, they do know that something is wrong, obviously because of some conditions in the atmosphere of their home. Other people are concerned about the value or the devaluation of their homes because of this-again fear of the unknown.
I would urge you to urge your officials to try if at all possible to arrive at an answer as quickly as possible.
We now go to Toronto and the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Weatherhead). He had this to say in a letter to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs:
- 1 do believe that a good case can be made for the fact that the government unwittingly enticed home owners to take advantage of the CHIP program and the home owners were relying on the government's implied assurances that the substance was not dangerous to their health-
The letter adds:
Every step should be taken to immediately accept replacing foam insulation in homes at the government's expense.
It should be pointed out that the hon. member for Scarborough West is chairman of the Ontario federal Liberal caucus. He said he is a Trudeau government supporter, but that he has to protect his constituents. While he is the first Liberal backbencher to speak out, he said "1 won't be alone".
Completing our roster of members who have had the guts to speak out publicly on behalf of their constituents in this issue, I turn to the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Cyr) who spoke in an adjournment debate on May 3, a few days ago. Referring to the Gaspe, he said:
The owners followed the directions given by the Government of Canada to save energy and applied for a grant to insulate their homes. Most owners who used area formaldehyde foam insulation are now facing a health problem and must find another place to live in and this is not easy in an area such as ours.
Mr. Speaker, even if the Government of Canada provided a $5,000 grant to remove that foam from the walls of a house whose owner is unemployed or is on welfare, where will this owner find the additional $10,000 to have the work performed? Even people who have permanent jobs but whose property was mortgaged to have that insulation put in can no longer afford to borrow at 20 per cent to have the foam removed from their walls and ceilings.
The hon. member for Gaspe told the House last week:
-I intend to participate in the debate on second reading of this bill in order to defend the interests of the people I represent here in this House, the victims of urea formaldehyde foam insulation, and especially those who are in a precarious financial situation.
I am looking forward to hearing the intervention of the hon. member for Gaspe.
When The Citizen or anyone else, including hon. members on the government side, mentions the word "compensation", total or otherwise, those of us who are on the front lines of the UFFI battle are constantly pursued about the dollar value of such a program. My answer is yes, the cost of restoring
victims' homes to being safe and saleable places will be expensive, and yes, it could amount to hundreds of millions of dollars; but I can never recall a bottom line where the health of this nation is concerned. I will say more about financing later, but this $110 million remedial program has now been scaled down by half for actual disbursement to homes with the foam. The other $65 million presumably has been used for testing, publicity, dosimeters-

speechtext:
The $55 million remaining is as useless to UFFI victims as the June 30, 1983, deadline to qualify for the grants.
There is no way to paper over this issue. Home owners know it, real estate agents know it, provincial governments know it and, having talked with hundreds of UFFI victims across Canada during the past 18 months, believe me, I know how desperate many thousands of innocent victims of *the foam crisis are for federal government assistance. They know how woefully inadequate this remedial bill is. They are looking to government for much more meaningful compensation for their shattered lifestyles.
I am particularly saddened and, indeed, sickened by letters and reports which flow into my office every week from UFFI victims all across Canada. One newspaper just yesterday carried a story of a couple in Downsview, Ontario, who watched their $135,000 home of 15 years being bulldozed because of urea formaldehyde foam insulation. With their home, this couple which had emigrated from Italy also watched their lifetime of hard work and cherished memories being demolished. Now they are starting over. They are building a new home and plunging into debt once again. Understandably, they are bitter and disappointed at an Ottawa government which had urged the country to save energy with insulation but which will not take its responsibility now. In a statement, which could be mirrored 100,000 times, the Downsview couple said:
They pushed us to put in the insulation, and now they want to wash their hands of it.
Worse, these people cannot be eligible for any financial help. They tore down their house. Now they do not qualify for aid, according to a spokesman for the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs. I find that an unconscionable abdication of this government's responsibilities, and I will have a recommendation to make in this regard in a few moments.
May 10, 1982

Let me put on the record the views of some Canadian home owners plagued with UFFI. Their own words speak volumes about the issue now confronting this Parliament. My office here on Parliament Hill has been in continuous touch with HUFFI- Home owners with Urea Formaldehyde Foam Insulation-group leaders across Canada who represent thousands of home owners with UFFI. The Minister talks about some of us who raise this issue as being deliberately politically partisan. I do not know or care what the politics of UFFI home owners are, but we are in constant touch with them, and they continue to bring to us the real stories of the home owners they represent. The minister talks about people like John Owen from Vancouver; Dr. Penny Tilby from Vancouver; Fred Palen from North Calgary; Stan Wilson from Regina; Glenn Markowski and Lloyd Maynard from Winnipeg; Ace Willsie, Pam Snow, Jim Inch and Margaret Vagalaid from Kitchener-Waterloo; Ms. Pat Clarke from Scarborough; Dr. Frank Spitzer from Toronto; Ed Smee from Hamilton; Lee Kennedy from London; Bob Ord from Welland; Rick Patten, Murray Coolican and Mrs. Pat Strickland from Ottawa; Len Cocolicchio and Mr. Larry Gee from Montreal; Madam Nicole Lamer and Yves Nantel from Ste. Therese, Quebec; Carl Wentzell from Riverview, New Brunswick; Mr. Mark Poirier from Halifax, Nova Scotia; and Danny Williams from St. John's, Newfoundland. Almost on a daily basis these people keep us informed on the progress and plights of many thousands of home owners.
Incidentally, I want at this time to pay a special tribute to my researcher, Mr. Sean Berrigan, who has become Parliament's unoffical ombudsman for countless UFFI organizations which have been springing up across Canada. Many of my colleagues in this House are aware of Mr. Berrigan's untiring dedication to the plight of UFFI home owners, whether individuals or vast organizations, across Canada. I just want to take this opportunity to thank him for his painstaking research for me and my colleagues in our collective attempt to gain justice for so many Canadians who have been so aggrieved.
I have a letter here to the aforementioned Mr. Larry Gee in Pointe Claire from A. E. LePage, a real estate firm, and this letter says it all:
It is certainly unfortunate that although all of these indications suggest a market value of $42,000, I feel that because of the type of insulation (i.e. urea formaldehyde foam) in your home it would be virtually impossible to market.
Since the insulation in your home appears to be impossible to remove without virtually removing the building, I would have to consider the building to be worthless. In fact it is a liability, as someone would have to spend money to effect its removal.
The land value in the area indicates that your lot because of its location should sell for $15,000; however the cost of removal of the building may have to be deducted from this amount.
That is the kind of financial situation Mr. Gee has ended up in as a result of this crisis.
I have here an open letter to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) from Felice and Frank Spitzer of Toronto. Mr. Spitzer is head of the Ontario HUFFI Association.
Naturally the most serious repercussion of this whole issue is that of health. In our particular instance, my husband has been severely affected with a sinus
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
problem. He was operated on just one and one-half years ago and is unfortunately no better. Naturally he suffers and as a consequence the normal routines of family life are somewhat hindered. It even goes so far as with tiny matters such as the fact that we cannot talk to him in the mornings while he has to rinse his mouth out for long periods at a time so that nobody can have any conversation with him until we actually sit down to breakfast.
The litany of health problems goes on and on.
I have here a letter to my colleague, the hon. member for Waterloo (Mr. McLean), from Donna, Wayne, Sue and Terry Gravelle of Waterloo:
Several days ago my husband went to see Dr. Wyse for pulmonary and allergy tests. He has been attending doctors for quite some time as he has had sore eyes, running ears and severe breathing problems. Dr. Wyse has stated he feels positive that his problems are caused by the UFFI in our home. He feels we should move out of the house because of Wayne's problems and the problems the rest of the family are experiencing. He has also stated he is willing to testify that he feels the foam is causing these problems.
Is there anything that can be done! WE ARE DESPERATE!
That is signed by Mrs. Donna Gravelle.
I have received a letter from a Mr. Peter Lake of Edmonton, Alberta who says:
My problem is as follows. I am faced with having to sell my house within the next 16 to 24 months for a work-related move. Since I have urea formaldehyde foam insulation in my walls, the marketability of my house is nil, and I am faced with the prospect of losing all of my equity and possibly being left with a mortgage to pay off as well. This would leave me with no chance to purchase another home in my new location as I would have no downpayment and, since I have already used my RHOSP eligibility, no easy way to save.
The Government has suggested a number of ways of making UFFI houses habitable with sealing and chemical absorbers, but clearly, the only way to make a house marketable is to remove the foam.
The Government has mentioned the possibility of (but has not yet promised) aid of up to $5,000 towards making UFFI homes safe, but I have received estimates of $15,000 to $20,000 to remove the foam. My house has stucco outside and plaster inside.
That letter raises a point that I think should be cleared up. Many Canadians are under the impression that if they qualify for a grant, if the level of urea formaldehyde warrants a grant, they will get the whole $5,000. While that is not nearly enough to remove the material from their homes, most people seem to think that they are eligible for that amount. I think that the minister and the government should make it clear to home owners who are applying for grants that they can get up to $5,000 but that they could receive a much smaller amount.
In the few minutes remaining to me, Mr. Speaker, I want to raise some questions and offer some recommendations to the government. Perhaps the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) can deal with these questions later in the debate or when he appears before the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs later in the week.
These are the questions that I should like to have answered. What about residents of buildings other than single family homes? Urea formaldehyde foam has been used as an insulation material in a number of apartment buildings, offices and commercial complexes. Is the government satisfied that it has a full list of such buildings and is it satisfied that it can accurately test levels of gas in the various segments of such buildings where people work and live? Then there is the question of

May 10, 1982
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
who is responsible for testing. Is that up to the person dwelling in a building or working in a building, or does the government accept the responsibility for seeking out and testing dwellings that are not owner occupied but which have been insulated with UFFI? If not, how can workers in office buildings or residents of apartment buildings find out whether they should have their place of work or residence tested? Who would pay the cost of such tests?
Then comes the matter of retroactivity to which I referred earler in the case of the couple from Downsview. Is compensation available to people who had UFFI removed from their homes because they or their families had fears of or had experienced a health problem? If so, how far does retroactivity extend-to the temporary ban, to the permanent ban or to the introduction of this bill, either last December or just a few days ago at the end of April? Do such people also have unlimited rights to sue in the courts? These questions are asked at virtually every home owner's meeting.
In terms of minimizing the financial risk of court action, does the government plan any special measures that would make it easier for victims of UFFI to launch suits in the court with a minimum of financial risk? What about health problems which emerge later? If the health problems emerge as a result of exposure to UFFI four, five or ten years ahead, will a legal obligation to pay compensation still be recognized by the Government of Canada?
There are a number of very critical questions that must be answered in connection with this bill but, I repeat, we must see the draft regulations before we know what course the government is going to pursue in implementing the bill, because that is where the guts of the legislation really lies.
Above all, we feel that more money must be made available to this program until the government gets beyond remedial aid to UFFI home owners and lives up to its responsibility for meaningful compensation. The $55 million is woefully inadequate when you consider the number of Canadians who are sick as a result of the mistake of the government. I would recommend that the bill and the remedial program be made retroactive. All Canadians who removed the foam or spent money trying to rectify the problem should be eligible from the date of the government's temporary ban on December 18, 1980. Any removal or structural corrections prior to that time would, presumably, be a matter for the courts to decide.
I would certainly recommend that amendments to be made to the bill to extend the life of the program or make provision for it to have long-term effects. The present expiry date is meaningless to those who are not experiencing problems now but in whose homes trouble may show up in the years ahead.
Let me conclude with my own personal thoughts on this UFFI crisis. Many describe it as a catastrophe. It started in 1980 and the early part of 1981 as a sleeper issue. Some people in government began to wake up to the realization that we might have a real problem on our hands, and some home owners began to experience a variety of problems directly attributable to urea formaldehyde foam. Many home owners
suddenly began to wonder what the growing controversy might do to the saleability of their homes. Government departments have been accumulating frightening evidence in the meantime, and there have been mounting fears from UFFI home owners about the effect on their health and on the sale of their property. An awakened and aroused public has escalated this issue into a national catastrophe.
We are faced with a problem without precedent. As elected representatives, we must do something about it. The people do not care which level of government is to blame. That is where the issue transcends partisan politics as far as the victims are concerned. A lot of Canadians are being hurt, whether because of their health or because of the value of their real estate or other economic reasons, and they are looking to government, any government, for help.
I want to close as I started, by suggesting that if you put all the heads of UFFI households in Canada in our two largest stadia there would be about 250,000 or 300,000 people there or roughly the population of Hamilton or Ottawa. They would all say what I have been saying this afternoon, that this UFFI mess is a disaster of the first order. Had all those Canadians been concentrated in one city would the federal government, the provincial governments and the municipal governments, not considered this mistake a true national disaster? Would all governments not have made this matter a top priority and quickly agreed on emergency measures on behalf of their afflicted taxpayers? It happens that these people are not all concentrated in one city but are spread from one end of the country to the other.
I do not minimize the responsibility of the prime offender in this UFFI mess, namely the federal government, but the provinces and the municipalities have a responsibility in terms of property taxes and re-assessment in light of this crisis. In short, governments must act at once, led by the federal government, to provide much more meaningful compensation than is set out in the bill.
It used to be said that the Canadian dream was to own one's home. For many thousands of Canadians that dream has turned into a nightmare. I think that this government and this Parliament must act at once to restore that Canadian dream for those home owners who have been afflicted with UFFI.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have waited long for this opportunity and it is with great anticipation that I take part in this debate. I would like to go back for a moment to comment on some of the minister's remarks, particularly his comment that he did not want to get involved in petty politics in considering this basic issue of urea formaldehyde foam insulation. I suggest to the minister that it is through the political process that a decision is made about the allocation of scarce and valuable resources. What that minister and that government have said continuously since the advent of this issue is that they are not willing to allocate adequate resources to meet the needs of a large number of home owners which arise from this very serious problem. The previous speaker tried to give some indication of the magnitude of the problem. Obviously, to some degree, it fell on deaf ears. On the other hand, perhaps if each one of those members were prepared to spend $1 in the minister's constituency, he would not only be driven away from his office as minister but would be driven away from this House altogether, which might be fair and just in view of the kind of program he has been supporting here today.
This issue has really two basic characteristics. One is that it is a national disaster. We are talking about homes being damaged and health jeopardized. It is an incredible situation in that if the problem were not scattered across the country, governments at all levels would leap to assist with substantial funds to rectify it. The other characteristic is the dishonesty of the program put forward. In presenting this thesis of dishonesty, I am suggesting that the following method is being used. Some time before 1977 a board was set up to approve this insulation material for use in homes. If the material was approved, a description was given of how the material was to be used. At the end of April, 1977, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) wrote to one of the industrial organizations involved and told them they would not be pressured into putting a substandard product such as urea formaldehyde foam into the homes of people. He was concerned about health problems and about it being a poor insulator, and he indicated there was no way the government was going to be pressured into supporting this material. Two months later that decision was completely reversed. The decision came not only from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in a telex to the companies involved, but misgivings were also expressed by CMHC and NRC officials. The only enthusiasts for this material were the manufacturers, and they sat on that board. No greater conflict of interest can be seen. That in my opinion was dishonest.
There is another aspect to it. When that decision came about, the Canadian Development Corporation acquired a share in a company which owned or controlled one of the manufacturers. The thesis that works now, is that there was political pressure to change that decision, especially on government officials on the board, and to gain approval for this product. So a company which was earning very little revenue and was close to bankruptcy, went on to become extremely
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
profitable as a result of this change of decision. Then, just before the ban, it was sold to another outfit, unsuspecting that the ban was coming into place and which, I assume lost its shirt on the deal.
The first thing we would like the minister to do is to hold a public inquiry to inquire into, under oath, the relationship between the CDC, Innocan, Rapco and Lorcon with a view to determining what the connections were between those organizations and the government officials in the approval of this product for use in Canadian homes. That is the first thing which must be done to lift this web of dishonesty which falls over the approval of that product. Second, I would like to point out that the program itself was put forward by the minister in very loud and vigorous terms in this House in an attempt to defend what the government has done and to curse the opposition for its petty political manoeuvring. The minister did nothing to alleviate the fears and concerns of people with that material in their homes. In fact, I suggest the government created a program designed to break the back of the political strength of the home owner's movement.
About two years after the approval, Mr. Speaker, the government of Saskatchewan asked the federal government to please ban the product. It fell on deaf ears again. The federal government was not interested in banning that product, in spite of the fact that Saskatchewan at that time was helping home owners with health problems by becoming involved in a relocation program. This is the second thing that we in the NDP would like to see the government do if it has any honesty. It should develop a relocation program so that those people with extremely high gas concentrations, who are suffering from health problems in their homes, can be relocated. Those who do not have the funds can be given a federal government grant to move out now before they and their children and other members of their family succumb to the health problems associated with that product.
These are two suggestions. A public inquiry would cost next to nothing but it might lift the web of dishonesty which appears to have fallen over this whole issue. The second suggestion is for a relocation program such as the one Saskatchewan became involved in long before the ban was ever announced. I notice the minister is off in some other area thinking of something else, but certainly those are two valuable suggestions.
Next we have the development of this program. The ban was eventually announced in December of 1980 after a great deal of persistence. But then no action was taken. There was a delay of a year before the government developed its program. Certainly a testing program was started and it took up a lot of time. Then the minister developed his answer to the Canadian problem: a $110 million program for home owners. But he announced it on December 23, a good time to avoid the political consequences of a tremendous inadequate program, the day before Christmas Eve. It was beautiful. A $5,000 grant, and a testing program, which, I assume, was based on the dosimeter approach to determine whether or not you had

0.1 parts per million in your home or had a health problem. Then you could qualify for a grant of up to $5,000. But there was a great delay. Groups began to form and, they believed that with some pressure they could get the government to realize and understand what their problem was. Then, lo and behold, an answer from the government.
It is interesting that when the minister announced the program he said that the next honourable thing to do would be for the provinces to become involved. They should get in and help, because the federal government was the only one doing anything. Really that was not true. Other governments were doing things. They were asking the federal government to ban the product before thousands more homes were filled with it. They were testing, and they were relocating. Not only that, they were asking the federal government to become involved in some of these activities. In no way did the federal government do that. But the minister could do something at this late stage. For example, when the minister put the program in place he wrote a letter to the provinces asking them whether they would like to participate in a program to help these home owners. One of the provinces indicated it would be interested and wrote for more details. However, the provinces read about the federal program in the newspaper. That is the kind of consultation in which the minister is prepared to engage. In the last week, I have visited five provinces and I have spoken to home owners, officials and consumer and corporate affairs ministers. They tell me they are prepared to help. But what kind of consultation do they get from this minister and this government? They get none. The reason is that it is basically a political manoeuvre on this government's part.
Third, we ask the minister to leave this House now and to call a federal-provincial conference of ministers responsible for the problem. 1 am certain that with any effort and some willingness to acknowledge at least some responsibility for the problem before us today, the minister would get the cooperation of provincial governments. Even some co-operation is better than what he is getting today. Provinces are indicating they are prepared to help. If the minister would call a federal-provincial conference I am certain that he would get those people here today. I urge him to do that. I urge him to develop consultation and a meaningful program, not an ad hoc, off-the-cuff program like the one he has developed and presented to us in this House. I hope the minister will have a little more respect for his provincial colleagues who are faced with the problem.
I have outlined three suggestions: the public inquiry, the relocation program and the federal-provincial conference. The minister will not walk away empty-handed. Throughout all of this time, there has never been proper consultation. Most of the officials and the ministers in the provinces would acknowledge that immediately.
It is interesting to look back on this matter. The minister announced the federal government had set up the Canadian General Standards Board, which was a program to show how to utilize the material. There must have been tremendous misgivings about this product. It appeared, until the end of
April, that there was no way it would receive approval because of reactions form NRC and from CMHC and even from what the minister wrote in the telex. But when the reversal came in the two-month period, it really appeared as though political pressure came into play in the decision. But when the decision came, it was not a simple one. Great concern was expressed about the product. As a condition of approval, the manufacturers were told to notify a customer directly the product was used of the terms and methods by which it should be used. There was also great concern about setting standards for installers in the field. Everyone knows that if you are in downtown Courtenay on Vancouver Island installing this material you do not have very much control over it. As a result, instead of following the directions laid down by the standards board, the manufacturers never sent out the required information to home owners, which was a condition of approval to use the product. When they failed to do that, approval was rescinded. But from what we can gather, one of the CMHC officials was under such tremendous political pressure to reinstate approval that two days later approval was given and the individual eventually resigned. That is a very serious situation. But there was no control on the installers in the field. Instead of using the material as recommended in exterior walls of wood frame houses, the installers poured it into masonry houses, into ceilings, into floors, and below ground level. In fact, they did everything conceivably wrong in the installation of UFFI. The chain of events is as follows. Officials representing the government on the standards board knew the material was hazardous. In some way they were coerced to recommend and approve the product, contrary to their best knowledge of what the dangers were. In laying down the conditions under which the material was to be used, they expressed serious concerns about being able to control them. Eventually we wound up with a dilemma.
Clearly, the government is responsible for that. It failed to act in the best interests of the consumer. It failed to provide adequate supervision. It failed to respond effectively to the problem we have before us today.
My colleague who spoke before me mentioned the serious concerns expressed by people. The minister said only a few complaints had been received in 1979 and only 100 were received the following year.
Let me recount an incident, which has been repeated hundreds of times. Urea formaldehyde foam insulation was installed in a family's home. The wife worked during the day and was home in the evening. She began to experience a very serious allergic reaction. The doctor could find no source and suggested that she was suffering from nerves. He advised her to quit work and spend more time at home. She did this, and her condition became worse. There was no medical tie to the problem because the people did not know what was in the home. The insulation had been installed by a company. Adequate information had not been given to the family. Eventually this family read in the newspaper that UFFI could
May 10, 1982

cause certain health problems. They confirmed they had UFFI installed in their home. They attempted to get information about it. They decided to have the UFFI removed, and their health problems cleared up immediately.
I sat down with a man at a kitchen table last Thursday. He is head of the UFFI home owners group. His wife and children had terrible reactions to his product. He told me that he could not wait for the government to decide what it would do and that he had had to get the stuff out of his house. He told me his house was covered with stucco. He rented a concrete saw, stripped the stucco from the outside of his home and before the foam was removed the concentration of gas had sufficiently dropped in the home so that the family's health began to improve. He had difficulty gathering the funds to perform this operation. However, he is now in the process of putting his house back together again. But this individual has some serious questions because the minister has said that removing the deleterious substance from his home, which resulted in his family's health improving, disqualifies him from receiving any compensation. If the minister were to do a fair and honest thing, he would make an announcement that those people who have removed the foam from their homes, whether before December 23, 1981, or after that date, will qualify for whatever grants are available. I would urge the minister to make that statement here today. People cannot sacrifice their families to the uncertainties surrounding this material.
I have put only two examples on the record, but there are many, many more. In the cities of Winnipeg and Vancouver, people are pulling the stuff out of their homes. These people are asking why someone who pulled this insulation material out of his home before December 23 should qualify for the grant when they cannot? I would urge the minister to make a statement tonight that those people who are removing this insulation now can be considered for grants.

Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was discussing some suggestions which the government might follow. 1 should like to return to that train of thought by referring to some of the problems we see in this legislation and in the over-all program of the government. The first one was generally a severe criticism of the consultation in which the minister was involved with provincial governments when in fact there was no consultation whatsoever. In fact, some provincial governments were willing to provide assistance. We suggested that the minister should call immediately for a federal-provincial conference of ministers responsible for the urea formaldehyde problem and attempt to develop a coherent and co-ordinated
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
program so that we could end the rather off the cuff or off-the-wall approach to the problem to date. I should like to elaborate on some other important features.
Earlier the minister indicated that there was not really a serious health problem with urea formaldehyde foam, when in fact there is very good evidence that it is a serious health problem. In some cases, family physicians have conducted various tests on their patients. Their patients, who suffered symptoms from being in UFFI homes, and those symptoms clear up when they moved from the home and then the symptoms reoccur when they went back to the house. The government of Saskatchewan was attempting to relocate people. Therefore, the second suggestion was to provide relocation assistance immediately to those people who were suffering severe reactions to the foam in their homes. It has been 14 months or 15 months since the ban was announced. Pensioners and lower income individuals in particular who cannot afford to relocate are still living in those homes. We urge the minister to improve the bill and to develop a relocation program quickly so that relocation assistance could quickly be provided when a physician decides that a home is unsafe for a family.
We also dealt with the serious concern of individuals with the entire approval system. The minister went into great detail to explain how the Canadian General Standards Board approached the process for the approval of urea formaldehyde foam insulation. However, in reality, if the documents pertaining to exchanges between ministers and other individuals were publicized, they would show that the National Research Council and the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources were extremely skeptical and seriously concerned about approving this material. This was not the case of the industry officials who were very eager to have the product approved. Suddenly we saw, after some changes within the Canadian Development Corporation and acquisitions that they made, that there was a rapid move toward approval of UFFI. Since that process has not been reviewed, the government should organize a public inquiry into that very question. There is an extremely good reason for conducting this inquiry. First, it would prove very helpful in any lawsuits which may develop and it would save home owners tens of thousands of dollars, if not hundreds of thousands, in investigative research. Therefore, those facts should be published in order to provide the public with information which they have a right to know. As I say, a public inquiry into that facet of the process is extremely important.
We advocate a public inquiry into the relationship between the Canadian Development Corporation and its subsidiaries as well as into the approval process of the Canadian General Standards Board.
The next area I would like to discuss is the question of research which has been conducted into this product. If there is any justification-which there is not-for the existence of this problem of failure to act quickly it would be that there is

May 10, 1982
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
really no solid foundation of information on urea formaldehyde and its potential effects on homes and people and what could possibly be done to alleviate the situation.
It is interesting to note that I asked a question in the House on April 20, concerning the research project. It appeared that there were problems with the safe level of concentration of gas and the level which the government would accept as a criteria for assistance. There was no clear understanding of what type of gases were developing in the UFFI or what the actual allergic agents were. Rather than answering the question, the minister stated:
I am surprised at the hon. member's question, because just before the Easter adjournment I sent all members of the House an information document which included a list of research projects started by the National Research Council of Canada and the Department of National Health and Welfare. I should be happy to send the hon. member some more copies.
Unfortunately, when we went back to review the document which the minister delivered, there were some very sketchy details about some projects. I telephoned his office, and one of his aides said that the minister made a mistake when he said that a list of research projects had been distributed before Easter. His department was currently making a list of projects initiated by the National Research Council and the Department of National Health and Welfare which would be ready "tomorrow", which was April 22, 1982. Therefore, on May 7, after a great deal of pressure was applied, the National Research Council finished and delivered a list of the research projects which seemed to have been undertaken. There must be more than appear on this list, but it does describe in some detail projects which had been undertaken by the National Research Council.
They seem to be widely varying projects but only one deals with the health question. The report from Bruce M. Small and Associates appears to be the only project dealing with the health question. He prepared a handbook on the sensitization effects of UFFI, and he was to investigate the research that had been done on chemical susceptibility UFFI. Basically, this has been the only information we have received on the adequacy of the research program. There appear to be 23 contracts but very little information on the medical effects. After having completed his study, Mr. Small seemed very concerned about the question of immunity. In his analysis of the research he believes that what appears to happen is that exposure to urea formaldehyde gas tends to break down a person's immunity system and therefore makes individuals more susceptible to disease. Whether or not that condition has been substantiated still requires addition research. Certainly the symptoms people experience from the presence of UFFI in their homes, the stated concerns of government and other public health officials as well as statements of those concerns in research literature would certainly be sufficient indications that we have, a serious health problem, contrary to what the minister says.
There is another study which was done by Professor Albert Nantel. He is a professor who is involved in toxicology at the Laval University. Professor Nantel made a presentation to the Lamoreux Commission on urea formaldehyde foam. I will read a short portion of what he had to say:
What I found was at first sight surprising and, at second sight, frightening. Whether it is formaldehyde itself or any other contaminant released in the ambiant air of these houses insulated with urea-formaldehyde, I had to come to the conclusion that something does produce a severe depression in the natural defence mechanism of their organism.
Again, he is talking about the body's immunity system. He also raised serious concerns about the fact that in some of the homes which he studied, with even less UFFI than 0.1 parts per million, symptoms were displayed at concentrations well below that figure.
It was pointed out that the standard of 0.1 parts per million was arrived at in a very arbitrary way from industrial standards in Europe and then transferred to domestic standards in Canada. This fact deserves more attention. Since normal, healthy individuals only spend up to eight hours a day in the working environment, it is difficult to see how the government could implement its entire program in Canada based on this standard of 0.1 parts per million in an industrial environment. We now have a standard of 0.1 parts per million in a domestic environment where there are elderly people, people with allergies, young children and families who are in the home for much longer periods than those workers in Europe. In many cases, women and children would get maximum exposure and children and elderly people in particular would be extremely vulnerable. Instead of the minister's developing a program based on a maximum of 0.1 parts of urea formaldehyde per million as the starting point of health problems, he should be seriously considering a program that would simply remove UFFI from homes which have it.
Professor Nantel goes on to say that 0.1 parts per million is not a good standard because there are many health defects which occur at lower levels than that. He suggests that the level be lowered and that UFFI should be considered to be a very serious health hazard. Apparently, Dr. Nantel is concerned about extending his research into this subject, and there is a very limited amount of medical research material coming forward. The government should be seriously looking forward at providing additional funding to Nantel and other individuals to examining these serious health hazards.
Another aspect, as we look through the list of research documents is the question of dealing with the building structure itself. The minister proposes to go around and measure concentrations in homes. When the dosimeter indicates a reading greater than 0.1 parts per million, he will then order a comprehensive test. Should the concentration be borne out, he will look at applications for remedial action, but the question remains as to what happens to homes which do not have levels 0.1 ppm or greater. As I understand it, he will either go through a remedial program in the high concentration homes and give people certificates saying their homes are certified safe for all time, or else, I presume, he will give those homes which measure less than 0.1 parts per million some type of safety certificate to tell the occupants that it is safe forever. However, in reality the testing program is very scanty and poor.

First of all, there is a real question concerning how people are handling dosimeters in the field. There is a question of the timing during this period of the year, delaying the testing program, from winter to late spring. When the windows and doors in homes are open, we do not know how the readings in the springtime will compare with those in the wintertime. When the temperatures in homes are up and there is a certain internal humidity and the gas concentrations will change. The timing of those readings is extremely important. The building structure itself, the trapping of moisture and the growth of fungus in the walls must be considered. Fungus might give off spores which penetrate the walls, making it possible for allergic reactions to be set off, reactions which could cause problems.
As well, at certain times of the year some areas in the house reach higher temperatures than other parts of the house. During the wet period in the winter, moisture might be trapped, beginning the rapid decomposition of what would appear to be stable insulation. We must consider the trapping of moisture, the breaking down of formaldehyde and the rotting of the wooden structure, which could weaken the structural integrity of the home. We must consider the question of corrosion in wires, nails and metals which, again, could not only weaken the structural integrity of the home but could also cause dangerous electrical problems. Then again, we must also consider the question of the release of gas other than formaldehyde. In short, there is a tremendous need for research into this area. There is a good possibility that the very real kind of testing program which has been developed, will probably catch only 10 per cent or maybe 20 per cent of the homes and will miss the problems in other homes which the minister claims are safe, and this is a serious concern.
Therefore, with the development of the government's program, I assume we will see strengthening of research. I do not think these are simply token programs. I think we will see a systematic development of research into these areas and the government will be prepared vigorously to pursue this research, especially into the question of the removal of the insulation from homes. As well, there will be work toward establishing the relation of health problems to exposure to urea formaldehyde gas and the possibility of the existence of other gases in that insulation which might be released and cause problems. It has been suggested that phosgene and several other fairly serious compounds are released. So in terms of the funding program and the development of a better approach, we would suggest to the minister that this research program is not adequate and that much stronger emphasis should be placed on health.
Quite a number of provincial home owner associations are considering bringing in people like Albert Nantel and other experts in the field to hold seminars with local physicians. These family physicians are very reluctant to relate the symptoms of their patients to formaldehyde gas. There is a very serious problem in getting enough expert information to physicians. Some home owner groups are attempting to do this. This is certainly the type of role the government should be undertaking through the Department of National Health and
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
Welfare to ensure that physicians have adequate information with which to deal with this problem. We have requested this of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss Begin) long before the ban was announced. So the research question is extremely important.
It is also rather interesting to note the government's position in the material that it has published to date. I wish to quote briefly from a document entitled "Building Practice No. 23" by R. P. Bowen, Shirtliffe and Chown. The preamble states:
This document has been prepared to meet the demand by consumers and contractors for guidance in solving problems related to urea formaldehyde foam insulation. The need to provide immediate information has not allowed for intensive research or extensive field trials of the remedial measures presented.
I think the salient point there is that most of the information coming forward is still pretty sketchy.
The second question regards the term "formaldehyde gas". As used in this document, it refers to the mixture of gases released by UFFI. Formaldehyde gas is usually predominant. Since the composition of gases may vary from product to product, the gas is difficult to characterize and might be called UFFI gas, so that we really do not know the product with which we are dealing or to which we are exposing people in homes, people such as the elderly, children and people with other problems. This is the entire document which people seem to be using as their guide for rehabilitating their homes. It goes through removal procedures, sealing and other procedures which will generally make their homes safe from the minister's certification standpoint. Let me simply read the National Research Council's position concerning what it recommends homeowners to do.
The National Research Council of Canada or any person acting on its behalf assumes no liability arising from the use of information contained in this document nor warrants that such use will be free from privately owned rights.
That statement is almost a disclaimer of responsibility for recommended procedures. There is a very clear need for a better base of information from which home owners can work. There is a definite need for clear information as to the need for removing that material from the home and making the home secure, as well as information regarding its effect on health. We need to know what is involved in this gas and its effects on human beings. I would urge that the minister very quickly move forward to resolve this problem.
It is interesting that the minister spent a great deal of time criticizing the American position on this matter. He takes great pride in saying that we were the first to ban it, but the government never should have approved it in the beginning. Once the government became aware of the problem, it allowed thousands of homes to be filled with the material. It finally put on a temporary ban and then a permanent ban. Then, when asked to set up a compensation program, to inform physicians of the problems, and to take an active role in informing home owners, it opted for a more passive, and inadequate program. The minister takes great delight in saying that we were the first, and that no one else was involved but us.

Just to bring my comments very quickly to a close, Mr. Speaker, I would draw attention to two last points. One of the findings which seems to be coming out of the research is that urea formaldehyde is an unstable compound. If we deal with only 10 per cent of the homes and if the minister is prepared to pay roughly $1,000 on an average to seal off that gas and reduce its concentration in homes, he should be paying out about $8 million from the program, if that guess is anywhere near correct.
The problem is that urea formaldehyde in safe homes will continue to degrade, break down and release formaldehyde gas. After the cutoff date of June, 1983 when this program is no longer continued, we will have a situation where other homes have a gas buildup and there will be health reactions. We have to look toward a program that covers all homes. The only way to be certain that we have covered all homes is for the government to guarantee that it will remove, without cost to the home owner, that material from the home. Basically, it was a federal government error.
The second point is the legal situation. Very early on the minister said it was not the fault of the government. If homes owners wanted to go after somebody to find fault, they should sue the manufacturers, suppliers or installers of this material. In every province in Canada there were attempts to explore legal action which the minister suggested they pursue. In fact, the minister was going to make an amendment to the Crown Liabilities Act in this bill so that accepting a grant would not bar a civil action. I wonder if the minister knew in the beginning that legal action was an impossibility. Those who have looked closely at the possibility see that civil action will cost tens of thousands, if not hundreds of thousands, of dollars in extremely complex law cases. There are statute of limitation problems and the difficulty of financing those legal actions. This makes it virtually impossible for victims to sue. The minister must have known this when he suggested civil action.
As an alternative, we suggest that the provincial and federal governments fund cases that groups might bring on behalf of a number of individuals. There is opportunity in British Columbia to sue under the trade practices act. Many individuals would like to launch a civil action against the manufacturer, and many would like to sue the federal government on the basis of the way this material was approved and the federal responsibility for setting proper standards and inspection procedures with regard to the installation of this material. The minister knew in advance that it was virtually impossible to launch civil action without help from the government.
In summary, we want a federal-provincial conference on the UFFI issue. This bill is hopelessly inadequate. There is the
possibility of good, solid consultation and the development of a co-operative national program to deal with this national disaster.
There should be a relocation program for those who have health problems because of the high concentration of gas in their homes. They should be relocated. That should be done by the federal government without bickering as to who will eventually pay the bill. Their health is at stake.
There is the question of what the minister should do today. Fair play would dictate that he should clarify the situation as to whether home owners who remove the foam after they have documented it, and kept the proper reasons, can receive the same treatment as those who remove the foam from their homes before December 23. That is only fair.
There should be comprehensive research funding for an individual like Nantel and others who have to provide a proper information base. This bill is hopelessly inadequate. There should be a public inquiry into the relationship and approval procedure between RAPCO, CDC and Innocan and the approval process to shed light on the serious questions being asked. That would provide assistance by cutting some of the costs of discovery in legal actions that will develop from this issue.
Finally, the bottom line in this question is that the federal government made a very serious mistake. It approved a substance which many of its officials knew was inherently unstable and dangerous. It is basically a federal responsibility, not that of anyone else. It is not the responsibility of the provincial government, the opposition, the home owners, or people standing in front of the minister's constituency office with placards and gas masks, not the responsibility of anyone but this government. It made the mistake, therefore, it owes the people compensation. The compensation should be for removal of the foam from their homes at no cost to the home owner.
This can be structured in such a way that there are priorities for removal, such as the elderly, those with health problems, those with children in the home, or any others in jeopardy. Second, people can be compensated through a variety of mechanisms. The minister should have the courage to bring forward proper amendments before the bill goes to committee so that members of the House and Canadians can look at those amendments. Those who have to move because of job changes or other reasons and face an enormous equity loss in their homes should be given priority to remove the foam and renovate the home. It should come out of buildings where there are school children, elderly people or others who are vulnerable. Beyond that, people could be given the minister's certificate that they can have the insulation removed from their homes at their convenience. This could be funded by a variety of mechanisms. The only way to wind up with a home in a safe, habitable home with every manner confidence whatsoever is to remove the foam and rehabilitate the home. That is clearly the answer.
