1 have one parting shot before terminating. It would be interesting to hear what the Conservative Party members would advocate it and when they ever come to power. Every party in this House should put, no pun intended, their chips on the table. The government indicated it is not prepared to go further with compensation. This is the extent of the allocation of scarce and valuable resources that they are prepared to make in this situation. I suggest to my colleagues on my right that it is time they put their program on the table. So that owners will know where they really stand on the issue.

Mr. Speaker, it is almost a duty to speak to Bill C-109, now being considered at second reading and intended to provide for payments to owners of dwellings insulated with urea formaldehyde foam. Considering all that has been said on the subject before, what was said today and what will probably be said tomorrow, I feel we should realize what formaldehyde gas is and the effects it may have on humans, as well as the straightforward and concrete action taken by the government since it became aware of the problems besetting people living in homes insulated with this product.
Mr. Speaker, formaldehyde gas is acrid and colourless, and exists in small quantities in the air we breathe outside. It emanates from a variety of sources including incinerators, engine exhausts and smog. Normally, air contains from 0.005 to 0.05 parts per million of this gas, although levels may be higher under unfavourable conditions. Formaldehyde gas may escape from urea formaldehyde foam insulation. The amount will depend on several factors, including the ambient temperature, humidity, the competence of the installer and the formula used in preparing the foam. In our homes, formaldehyde gas may come from sources other than home insulation. For instance, smokers are exposed to higher levels of the gas, since cigarette smoke contains 40 parts per million. Particle board and plywood, gas stoves and space heaters and also fumes of cooking oil may also raise levels of formaldehyde gas in the home. There are a variety of symptoms associated with exposure to formaldehyde gas, and they depend, of course, on the levels to which a person is exposed. If levels are low, there are no negative consequences. However, some people may be more sensitive than others to the presence of formaldehyde gas. Health and Welfare Canada has suggested a level of 0.1 parts per million as an acceptable standard for the quality of air inside the home.
The standard was established according to a safety principle, to protect the elderly, the young, those who are ill as a result of other causes, and the general public. Most people should not have any symptoms at this or lesser levels. Many people exposed to levels of up to 0.25 parts per million, that is, two and a half times the accepted level of concentration are not even aware of it. However, people who are particularly
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
sensitive react to the presence of formaldehyde and feel a slight irritation of the eyes, nose and throat. When exposed to levels exceeding 1.00 parts per million, that is, at least ten times the accepted level of concentration for ambient air in the home, most people feel obvious discomfort and a number of symptoms may appear, such as irritation of the eyes, nose, throat and respiratory passages, dryness in the mouth, headaches, nose bleeds and insomnia. It was also found that certain people develop allergies when exposed to formaldehyde solutions and also that formaldehyde gas, even at low levels, could aggravate asthma attacks.
Although formaldehyde has been used since the last century, until now there has been very little research on its long term effects. A year and a half ago, it was discovered that formaldehyde caused a rare form of cancer in the nasal passages of rats and mice. However, the same type of cancer has not been observed in humans, not even in workers exposed to fairly high levels of formaldehyde gas. Nevertheless, a number of research projects are now underway, including complete epidemiological research programs, for the purpose of finding out whether there is a high cancer mortality rate among certain groups, for instance, undertakers and workers in the chemical industry. These groups are exposed to fairly high levels of formaldehyde gas. Any substance that causes cancer in laboratory animals should be considered dangerous to man, unless it is clearly established that the human body is able to break down or make a different use of this substance. This is a basic principle where health protection is concerned, and it is generally recognized, for instance, in the legislation on food and drugs. At the present time, researchers are trying to establish why formaldehyde causes cancer in certain animals.
If we assume that the risk of cancer is the same for men as for rats and mice, we can presume that the maximum additional risk of cancer in the air containing some .05 part per million of formaldehyde gas is equivalent to that incurred by smoking a cigarette per week, the risk incurred at a level of .1 parts per million of formaldehyde gas being less than a third of a cigarette smoked daily, Mr. Speaker.
Let us see now what happens under working conditions. In that environment, to establish the maximum concentrated level of formaldehyde which could be considered as being consistent with the security standards for homes, the Department of National Health and Welfare has examined the medical files of individuals usually exposed to formaldehyde gas at work. The actual threshold in an industrial environment is two parts per million for healthy adults working 48 hours weekly. Medical files kept for long periods show no sign or symptom of asthma resulting from formaldehyde exposure. A study of medical books and articles does not show any such case either. However, the Department of National Health and Welfare does not exclude the possibility that asthma sufferers, following formaldehyde exposure, could become more prone to other allergies.

May 10, 1982
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
Let us deal now with the conditions in our homes. In an average home, one can find babies, youngsters, sick persons or old people and since many could be living there 24 hours a day, the acceptable standard in an industrial environment, that is two parts per million, is deemed to be unacceptable for residents. Several health specialists suggest the application of a 10 factor and adaptations that take into consideration the likelihood of increased exposure in those houses.
The Department of National Elealth and Welfare has decided to provide an additional security margin by setting a standard twenty times lower than that used in the industry. Mr. Speaker, the Canadian standard is similar to that in other countries. For example, the governments of Norway, the Federal Republic of Germany, of Australia as well as the American Association for Industrial Health have set at . 1 part per million the maximum allowable level of formaldehyde in the air inside a house insulated with urea formaldehyde foam.
What is urea formaldehyde foam? It is an isolating substance which is a compound made up of urea formaldehyde resin, an acid used as a hardening agent-usually phosphoric acid-and a gas-most of the time, compressed air. The substance is prepared on the premises where it is to be used. It is injected through hoses into the walls of a building where it hardens. It becomes therefore solid isolation. Before it is injected into the walls, the freshly made foam is some 75 per cent water, and during the hardening process, once it has been injected, formaldehyde is given off. Mr. Speaker, urea formaldehyde was used for the first time as an isolating substance in the early sixties. It has been used increasingly ever since throughout the world. Today, it is used mostly in Germany, Britain, Sweden, Italy, Switzerland, Spain, France and South Africa. It is also available in the United States, except in Massachusetts and Connecticut where it is banned. Canada and Israel were the only two countries to take it off the market.
Late in 1977, following a request made by the CMHC, the Canadian General Standards Board set up interim standards for the insulating foam. This Board makes decisions based on consensus. The Board is made up of 10 representatives from the industry, 9 from the Federal Government, 4 from British Columbia, Alberta, Ontario and Quebec, the four provinces which have agreed on standards for urea formaldehyde foam insulation. It is the industry's duty to meet these standards. Following the Canadian General Standards Board's decision, the Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation accepted with the utmost reserve the use of this insulating substance which was added to the list of authorized substances under the Canadian Home Insulation Program, but only after the CMHC had brought this product to the attention of the Board and emphasized the precautions which were to be taken during the home insulating process. The Corporation even imposed the following conditions:
Installation specialists had to be trained. Second, a brochure explaining the installation process had to be given to the consumers before work started in their home. It behove Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation to provide adequate information to consumers about the material used to insulate their home. Third, the product was not to be used to insulate ceilings, floors or basements. It could only be used in hollow spaces between the walls of wood-frame houses. It could only be used in walls where the foam could dry rapidly. It could only be installed when the outside temperature was within the prescribed limits. The manufacturers had to form an association. Mr. Speaker, these are the precautions taken by a government agency following representations or comments showing concern over the use of the foam. Unfortunately, the product was installed in homes with brick walls, aluminium siding or other types of siding which prevent the gazeous components of the product to escape outside the building. The people inside the building are then seriously exposed to the hazards of urea formaldehyde, which is the main cause of the problems or the illnesses which I described earlier, namely eye, nose and throat, and sometimes skin irritations. After reading the first international reports warning of the health hazards related to urea formaldehyde foam insulation, the hon. Minister of National Health and Welfare of Canada (Miss Begin) established a committee of experts on UFFI to prevent any risk from this product, and soon afterwards, the government banned the sale of the product under the Hazardous Products Act. In its final report published in April 1981, the committee came to the following conclusion:
The ban should not be lifted as long as the industry is not able to demonstrate to the appropriate government agencies that is has developed a stable and definitive product.
Early in June 1981, the cabinet announced that it had asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouel-let) to implement a government action program and direct and co-ordinate the activities of all federal departments in this regard. On June 15, 1981, the Information and Co-ordination Centre was created as an integral part of the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs to inform the public, administer the inspection of a national sampling of homes and provide federal-provincial co-ordination. In fact, consumer protection standards are set by the provinces. They must ensure compliance with these standards and several provinces have their own insulation program. On June 10, 1980, the hon. Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs sent a telex to his provincial counterparts informing them of the federal initiatives concerning foam insulation and asking them to appoint a representative to co-ordinate activities with the Canadian government. As you can see, Mr. Speaker, it cannot be said that the government of Canada has never even warned the provincial governments about the problem which could be related to this insulating foam. During the federal-provincial conference held in September 1981, the Minister of Consumer
May 10, 1982

and Corporate Affairs asked the provincial governments to accept their own responsibilities. On that occasion, he reminded them about his request over a year before at the federal-provincial conference in Saskatoon, in June 1980, and which I have just mentioned.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to quote from a statement made at that time by the Canadian minister. He said:
A product of concern to us is urea formaldehyde foam. There have been enough consumer complaints concerning formaldehyde vapours to be concerned about short-term and long-term effects on health from exposure to the product. The problem stems partly from faulty application at the foaming stage. In order to assess consumer hazards from formaldehyde exposure, the National Research Council is setting up a program to measure formaldehyde concentration in a number of residences that were insulated with the product. The Canadian Department of National Health and Welfare also established an advisory council made up of health experts outside the government that have been instructed to evaluate potential toxic effects of the inhalation of the product at the concentration level found in actual homes.
The minister went on to say:
Over and above health considerations, faulty application of the product can have significant economic consequences for consumers. Because of the fragmentation of that industry, consumers have a hard time recouping the costs of faulty installation. Indeed, we find in that industry resin manufacturers, specialized firms that mix the product and others that distribute it, and also installers. The latter often are small contractors unable to assume the costs of redoing a faulty installation, which costs can range from $15,000 to $35,000.
We find that the product as such and the installation work are two important factors in the safety problem deriving from cellulosic insulators and urea formaldehyde based insulators. Regulations concerning the contents of the product are already in place in the case of cellulosic insulators, and it may become necessary to ban or regulate urea formaldehyde insulation, depending on the results of current studies.
The minister concluded:
In any event, it seems essential that provinces take steps, at the installer training and certification levels, to ensure their qualifications and reduce safety and health hazards to consumers that could derive from the toxic and fireproof properties of such products. I would therefore ask you to convey the message and the contents of the discussion we are going to have to your colleagues in charge of those matters in each province.
As you see, Mr. Speaker, the state of the matter has always been of prime concern to the government, and particularly the minister in charge. Later on, a whole series of tests was developed to assess what I would call our homes' health condition. That check started on August 24, 1981. Of course, priority was given to homes whose owners reported health problems or uncomfortable levels of formaldehyde vapour. We inspected 2,400 homes and on October 31, the operation was completed and reports were tabled. For the benefit of all, I would like to say a few words of the Hazardous Products Act. Under that act, a manufacturer can appeal a government ban on a product and request that a board of review be established. In February 1981, the Energlobe company in Philipsburg, Quebec, requested that urea formaldehyde foam installation be referred to such a board. Under the act, the government had to proceed, and did so. The board is chaired by Mr. Jacques Lamoureux, from the Montreal law firm of Lamoureux et
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
Rousseau. The other board members are Mr. Benjamin Lu, professor of chemical engineering at the University of Ottawa, and Dr. Robert Sutherland, a Toronto physician and industrial health consultant. A final decision on the product cannot be reached until such time as that board has given its verdict. In the meantime, the product is kept off the market. As soon as the report has been received, the government will of course make it public. So, without even waiting for the results of the report, the government has gone ahead and proposed an assistance program for those people whose homes have been insulated with urea formaldehyde foam.
I believe some of my colleagues will give you the details of the assistance programs the government is offering Canadians.
I should also like to point out that, while the government was offering citizens whatever help they need to improve their situation, it was also calling for some involvement on the part of the provinces. Despite repeated requests, the provinces still refuse to give any direct assistance to the owners of houses insulated with urea formaldehyde foam. In fact, the provinces that had been offering testing facilities have now discontinued that service. All the provinces have been approached and invited to co-operate in a program aimed at training and registering insulating contractors. Three western provinces only have replied, two of them in the affirmative, and the third, in the negative. The New Brunswick government has offered a $40,000 subsidy to the UFFI Homeowners Association. The Quebec government is also implementing a temporary program in four points: medical tests, level of UFFI concentration in walls, a very limited aid to relocation and corrective measures assessment. Therefore, the almost complete indifference of provincial governments is evident. Being responsible for the quality of products, it is their duty as well as that of the federal government to protect Canadians. And once again, to say that the government of Canada has not since the beginning been concerned with the health of the people and adequate means to help them, is just not true.
I repeat that the government has assumed its responsibility with courage and that by banning the use of this foam it has given Canadians increased protection. Even without any legal obligation the government has set up a program to assist home owners. This program's objective is to reduce UFFI emanations to a bearable level, at which those home owners can safely live again in their houses. Mr. Speaker, I think that the program brought forward along with the bill now under consideration is very important and very urgent. A number of citizens are waiting for the government's help and in my opinion, it is in the interest of every hon. member to see that the delays which are already extremely long are reduced to a minimum in order to meet, as soon as possible and in the most efficient way, the needs expressed by the people who are experiencing serious problems.

May 10, 1982
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act

Mr. Speaker, the bill we are debating here this evening, Bill C-109, an act to provide for payments to persons in respect of dwellings insulated with urea formaldehyde foam insulation, is a very important one. It actually should have been introduced months ago as we have had a lot of information, going back to 1960, as to the effects of urea foam. There are home owners all across Canada, as well as apartment dwellers and office workers and people in schools, who are going to welcome some type of action and compensation from the government so they can have some peace of mind. The minister should have detailed the amount of compensation more clearly in this legislation, as many people have already spent thousands of dollars in removing the insulation. I was at a public meeting two weeks ago in Winnipeg on this problem. A representative of the NDP government attended. He did not come forward with any sound information as to how Manitoba was going to help these home owners, and he received a very rough time from the gathering that evening. So if the provinces are going to become involved in providing compensation, I hope they come forward with some concrete plans in the near future.
The hon. member for Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) stated earlier that if the Conservatives formed the next government he was worried about whether they will live up to any commitments made. I can assure him that the Conservative government will live up to all of the commitments in this or any other bill with regard to full compensation for the home owner and anyone else who has problems with this insulation. I would like to congratulate my colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott), who has shown real leadership in the House and done exhaustive research in regard to this problem. He has probably done more than anyone to get the minister to move on this problem.
Home owners in Manitoba with this insulation, Mr. Speaker, have been patiently waiting for satisfactory compensation from the Liberal government. The president of the Manitoba UFFI Association, Glenn Markowski, is to be commended for the yeoman service he has undertaken to assist all Manitoba UFFI home owners. But he cannot accomplish anything on his own. That association has been hoping the minister would recognize the seriousness of the problem and the many hardships that home owners are being made to endure. It is becoming apparent that the Liberal government does not have the concern for the health and wellbeing of Canadians, which it has stated so many times it has, because it has taken so long to bring this bill forward. Why do people have to see their families suffer medical problems which have become so serious that people are having to wear gas masks to enter their homes? This actions was taken on the advice of a federal government employee, but it did not ease their problem or get rid of it; it only disguised it. Still encountering health problems is a Montreal couple who moved from their hard earned home to an apartment as a temporary arrangement. The same couple is in the process of moving back. Their hard-earned money is tied up in their home, but they are not moving back to live in this
house; they are having to move into their garage. Another couple has had to move into a mobile home parked in the driveway of their uninhabitable home.
Now, Mr. Speaker, acute and chronic health effects can and are happening. Individuals, as I am sure you are aware, vary in their reaction to formaldehyde gas exposure. Respiratory problems, eye, nasal and throat irritations will occur at different levels of exposure in different individuals. If a normal, healthy individual reacts to these gases, have you the evidence to allow you to set standards for the general population, which includes young children, the elderly, the infirm and pregnant women?
On April 20, in the House of Commons, the minister responsible brushed off all calls for the federal government to do more to help the victims of formaldehyde gas. Is this minister still insisting there is no real problem here? I believe that the government is attempting to divert public attention from the serious implications contained in the committee's final report of April 23, 1981. This report notes that UFFI is an unstable material of variable composition, which can break down and release formaldehyde gas. Formaldehyde is an irritant to the eyes, skin and breathing passages, and exposure to it can produce allergic responses in sensitive individuals. It has also been shown to produce cancer in laboratory animals.
On February 10 of this year the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) replied to a question asked by my colleague, the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), that:
-the Canadian government does not admit any legal responsibility in this matter.
On humanitarian grounds only the government decided to take action and assist on the basis of the government's responsibility for national health. How can the minister stand in the House and calmly say the government does not admit legal responsibility after approving UFFI in 1969, after tests had clearly shown it was a health hazard? Even as early as 1960 West Germany had proof it was a health hazard. The Liberal government approved UFFI in 1969 and withdrew its approval in 1970. The government approved this same material for a government funded grant program in the face of opposition from government agencies and departments in August, 1977. As an individual and an elected Member of Parliament, I would like to know how it is that a product which lost government acceptance previously due to instability was accepted for a nationwide home insulation plan, and why, after it was accepted, sponsored grants were given to encourage Canadians to use this insulation. How can the government now say calmly that it is not its responsibility?
It really is not necessary to conduct studies and reports on the health hazards of urea formaldehyde foam insulation. Between 1960 and 1981, 13 studies were completed on this same subject. These studies proved UFFI hazardous. A number of these studies were conducted by the Department of National Health and Welfare.
May 10, 1982

I will take a couple of minutes to document some of the studies that have already been conducted. First, was West Germany in 1960. In 1974 the Department of National Health and Welfare requested to review the material. In 1978, the head of chemicals and fuels safety in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs stated that exposure could lead to medical problems. In 1978, the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources stated that a federal committee investigating found there was potential damage to children and old people from long-term exposure. In 1978, the United States called for a stop of all UFFI sales, and pressed manufacturers to have health warnings on foam insulation contracts. In 1979, lab tests showed a link between UFFI and cancer rats at low emission rates. In 1979, there was a complete ban on UFFI in the United States after eight months of study. There was no response from the Department of National Health and Welfare at that time. In 1980, a report of the Department of National Health and Welfare was submitted and the minister announced a temporary ban on UFFI. In 1981, the Department of National Health and Welfare continued its ban on UFFI. Again, in 1981, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) appointed a review board and the United States confirmed that low doses of UFFI caused cancer in rats. Also in 1981 the National Research Council warned home owners of dangers. We have had many studies, Mr. Speaker. Now is the time for action, not more studies.
It is now a proven fact, which does not have to be proven again, that UFFI is hazardous to health. We need remedial action now. Is the government spending enough money on remedial action? The answer is no. Is the government spending more money on more studies to prove facts that have been proved so many times by so many reports and studies? The answer is yes.
Here is the current status report from the Department of National Health and Welfare on projects that are in operation or are under active consideration and the money that will be spent to prove a well-known proven fact, namely, that urea formaldehyde foam insulation is a health hazard. I say these reports and studies are a complete waste of money. We already know the results of UFFI in our Canadian homes. This is another example of the total disregard the Fiberal government has for federal spending. I say this money should have been put toward a better use, such as assisting home owners' associations deal with these problems. Better still, this money should have been used to assist home owners to get rid totally of this hazardous product from their homes.
As part of the grants contribution program in support of consumer groups, such as the Manitoba Home Owners' Association, which is administered by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, home owners' associations are to receive financial assistance. This financial assistance is supposed to provide assistance and service such as inquiries into the nature and extent of the problems caused by UFFI in their area. To do this, people have to travel in and around the Winnipeg area. Names, addresses and telephone numbers of each home owner have to be collected and given to the government UFFI centre. Questionnaires are to be circulated by the association to each and every home owner. Telephoning, telex
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
and advertising have to be undertaken. Halls and offices for meetings have to be rented to keep home owners informed. Photocopying has to be done and postage has to be paid so that members can receive the most up to date information by mail. These are just a few of the duties to be undertaken by home owner associations such as the one in Manitoba.
The government is proud of the fact that it is funding home owner's groups. It is funding these groups with the hope that it will cut down on work having to be done by government offices. For this service, which would cost the government millions to do it itself, what is paid in the form of a grant to the Manitoba Home Owners' Association? The Manitoba Home Owners' Association received a grant of $7,000. This $7,000 is expected to compensate for the time, travel, equipment, office work and every other detail required to assist approximately 2,000 Manitoba home owners receive assistance from the federal government. This is to correct an error that the federal government is responsible for instigating, but it is now saying "The Canadian government does not admit any legal responsibility in this matter." This $7,000 to Manitoba home owners works out to $3.50 per home. What does the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs expect Manitoba home owners to accomplish with this grant of $7,000 which breaks down to the grand total of $3.50 per home? What is the minister's rationale behind the granting of this paltry sum? The Manitoba home owners requested $20,000, and this by far was not unreasonable to look after the interests of 2,000 home owners. But they received just $7,000.
What is the solution? Is the answer that home owners just lost out if they happen not to be living in the minister's own province of Quebec which received a grant of $40,000? Maybe Manitobans would be better off if they all moved to Ontario, which received a grant of $39,000. This figure is for the province of Ontario. It does not account for the fact that Ottawa received a grant of $30,000. These two figures add up to a total of $69,000 in grants for the province of Ontario.
Will the minister explain loud enough for all 80,000 concerned home owners with UFFI in their homes what they have to do to receive a fair share of the money allotted to home owners' associations? Maybe the minister would like to explain what he could accomplish with the grand total of $3.50 per home when all Canadians know how this government procrastinates. How long will it be before this issue is settled? What would the minister be able to accomplish on this size of grant?
On February 10, 1982, my colleague the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott), the Conservative Party spokesman on the subject of UFFI, asked the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs if he would reconsider a much more meaningful compensation to owners of those many homes that are absolutely worthless. The minister replied that he was receiving positive responses to the very important and significant contributions by the Canadian government toward helping the victims of this product. Are all the minister's responses coming from the province of Quebec?

May 10, 1982
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
Let me just take a moment to review these "significant contributions by the Canadian government." The first one I have just discussed, that is, the significant contribution of $3.50 per home for the province of Manitoba to keep informed about what that province is supposed to be doing to receive assistance and, at the same time, to keep itself informed of the significant contributions by the Canadian government as the government announces them.
The second one occurred in December, 1981. The Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs announced that CMHC had been consulting with the real estate and mortgage and property insurance community whose activities had affected the owners of UFFI homes, in order to ensure that lending institutions continue to finance and renew mortgages on homes containing UFFI.
This also is one of the "significant contributions by the Canadian government". If CMHC had been successful in its dealings with these companies, which it was not, to whom would the home owners be able to sell? Who would want to own one of these health hazardous homes? Large mortgage insurers and lenders such as the Toronto Dominion Bank, the Nova Scotia bank and Canada Trust have now announced they will not handle mortgages on these homes. Where is the government's significant contribution in this area? The third but by far the biggest "significant" contribution by the Canadian government was when it announced that it will provide home owners with up to $5,000 tax free for necessary remedial action. The maximum payment to be made is $5,000. It is supposed to compensate home owners for problems arising from the insulation of their dwelling places with urea formaldehyde foam insulation. I do not have any idea how the government could have come up with this ridiculous figure- $5,000 will go nowhere toward correcting this very serious problem.
A family in Winnipeg has spent $8,000 to date to correct its problem, and a family in Verdun has received an estimate of $20,000 to remove the insulation from its home. In the meantime, this family is living in its garage after having tried to live in its hard-earned home while wearing gas masks. Some home owners have reported spending as high as $30,000 to have this insulation removed. The hon. member for Hamilton-Went-worth gave an example earlier today of a $ 135,000 home in the Toronto area which had to be demolished because there was no way in which the problem could be corrected. Will the minister provide $135,000 to that family? I hope he comes up with some answers. This money has to be spent either because the house is unsaleable otherwise or because adverse health effects make it essential. The "significant" contribution by the Canadian government of $5,000 toward a possible cost of between $10,000 and $30,000 to remove the foam is one of the contributions to which the minister says he is receiving a positive response. The government's contribution is a woefully inadequate drop in the bucket and an approach that comes too late. My party feels that the government should give fuller compensation both medically and financially to home owners.
Governments around the world have been conducting research since 1960. The government is responsible; it approved this insulation for use in Canadian homes and apartment buildings. The government encouraged home owners to insulate with this material by offering them a government-approved CHIP grant to insulate their homes with urea formaldehyde foam insulation. Now the government is claiming no responsibility or very little responsibility.
I say that the government is responsible. I say that all these studies, reports, investigations and tests which the government is conducting are useless. I say that the government is responsible for this hazard to health and the hazardous financial situation in which approximately 80,000 Canadian home owners find themselves. I can do no less than insist at this time that the government accept full responsibility for once in its life and make fuller compensation to these long-suffering Canadian home owners who put their trust in the government and are now being told that they have to sit and suffer. They have lost, and it is up to the House to see that they are fully and properly compensated for the problems with which they have had to live over the past 14 or 15 months. It has been an absolute disgrace and a burden upon these 80,000 Canadians.

speakeroldname: Hon. Flora MacDonald (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are times when one is asked to respond, either as an individual or as part of an organization, or even as a country, to a crisis which can take place in a very short period of time. We are facing one at the present time with regard to the Falkland Islands crisis. If anyone had asked a couple of months ago what we would be discussing in our homes and in news reports from the capitals of the world, very few people would have suggested that the Falkland Islands would have dominated the newscasts.
There are other crises which are also being discussed, one of them right across Canada. It has been discussed for some time now, but in fact two or three years ago UFFI was simply not known. Nobody would have recognized what was urea formaldehyde foam insulation or the acronym which we have now come to accept as a household word, UFFI. It is not a very nice household word, either.
It is a dirty four-letter word.

Yes, as my colleague says, it is a dirty four-letter word, one which we would much rather never have heard in our whole legacy of the English language. But now it is there as an acronym and as something which has become very familiar to Canadians across the country. It is there as part of another program for which we use a similar acronym, CHIP, the Canadian Home Insulation Program. UFFI and CHIP go together. Of course the minister does not think that they go together, but they are linked together in the bill. There is no way that they can be separated, regardless of what the minister has said.
We are examining Bill C-109 tonight which concerns restitution to persons encouraged by the government to use
May 10, 1982

UFFI in their homes. It is interesting to note that the legislation in Bill C-109 was promised last December and that on May 10 the government finally introduced the bill for second reading. The government could not begin to grasp the urgency which so many people feel about this issue. What we have before us is a bill which unfortunately is too little and too late for home owners who accepted the fact that the federal government knew what it was doing when it recommended that urea formaldehyde foam insulation was acceptable and government-approved insulation for use through the government's Canadian home insulation program. They knew that the government had recommended it and approved it.
On the other hand, the government had been warned as far back as March 18, 1977 and again on May 18, 1977 by Dr. Ian Efford, director of the energy conservation branch of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, that UFFI should not receive governmental approval. We must ask why he did that five or six years ago.
He gave that warning to the government because of his concern of possible structural damage to buildings in which that kind of insulation would be installed. Nevertheless, regardless of his warnings, the insulation was approved by CMHC for use in the Canadian Home Insulation Program in September 1977. Even after that some government officials continued to investigate the properties of UFFI because they were suspicious that its use could result in structural damage to homes or, worse still, that it could result in health problems for human beings in the homes in which is was being used. Given the possible implications of the use of UFFI, of which the government now pleads ignorance, the government, the minister and CMHC put it forward as one of the insulation alternatives for the Canadian Home Insulation Program.
The federal government brought CHIP into being and suggested alternatives or various types of insulation which could be used for insulation purposes. It did not go out and demand that everyone should have to use UFFI. That is not the way the government went about it. It merely suggested it as an alternative. It encouraged it by listing it with government programs. It placed the weight of the government's credibility behind it.
Now the government has the unquestioned moral, and perhaps even legal responsibility to accept the consequences of its decision to make UFFI one of the government's approved alternatives for the CHIP insulation program.
Is the minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet) about to assume his responsibility for the actions he took? Not on your life. On February 10, 1982, in response to a question by my hon. colleague, the member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs had the audacity to say this, in reply to one of the many questions about UFFI posed by members on this side:
We have always maintained that the Canadian government does not admit any legal responsibility in this matter.
He went on to say in his answer:
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
-we have decided, on humanitarian grounds, to take action and assist them on the basis of our responsibility for national health.
Humanitarian grounds my eye. The minister and the government are shirking their responsibility. They will blame anyone. They will blame the provincial governments, the home insulators and they will blame the very home owners themselves who are the victims of this use of UFFI. They will blame anyone for the government's disastrous mistake of judgment and, I might add, its carelessness in this issue.
What do we have before us as a result of this continuing tragedy of errors-not comedy of errors but tragedy or errors? What we have before us is a bill which allows $55 million for partial compensation to a very minimal number of Canadians. It is a very minimal number of those estimated 100,000 Canadians who own homes which have been insulated with urea formaldehyde insulation foam.
Bill C-109, which is the one under consideration tonight, allows home owners who qualify to receive up to $5,000 in tax free grants to help compensate for the problems caused by UFFI. That compensation is a mere drop in the bucket for what home owners really require. In order for a home owner who finds himself in this disastrous mess to receive a grant, he first must fit into one of two categories. He must first have his home tested to determine whether the home contains more than 0.1 parts of formaldehyde per million parts of air. This is regarded as the maximum safe level, according to the Department of Health and Welfare. The other alternative is that he just have a doctor's certificate to prove that any health problems he or his family are suffering from are related to urea formaldehyde foam insulation.
The number of UFFI home owners who qualify under these two qualifications will indeed be minimal compared to the 100,000 UFFI victims who all deserve compensation for the federal government's blunder. They all deserve to be considered. This bill will only allow the consideration of a very few who find they can fit into those narrow categories.
Another problem one sees when examining this bill is that the regulations by which the above mentioned criteria for qualification are determined are not even included in the bill. Before passage of this bill it is incumbent upon the government and imperative that we see the regulations by which eligibility and the level of payments are to be determined. The minister has had precedent in the House for having regulations presented beforehand when a bill is in passage. At least he should take that minimum step to help the people who will apply under the regulations of this bill.
I ask the minister: what are the necessary criteria by which a physician is expected to prove that health problems are related to UFFI? How is the doctor going to determine that? As an example, I will give the minister the instance of a man in my riding who recently developed throat cancer. He has now had UFFI in his home for two years. This gentleman also smokes. How can a doctor be sure that the cancer can be attributed to either his smoking, to UFFI or to a combination of the two? What are the criteria by which that doctor is to

May 10, 1982
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
determine the origin of the cancer that this man has developed since UFFI could very well play a major part in it?
It is also very important to see the regulations so we know the exact process by which a UFFI home owner can receive a compensation grant under Bill C-109. I mention the fact that it has taken six months to bring this bill before the House since the minister first mentioned it. However, if you look at the bill, you can easily see that the whole process of application, inspection, testing and analysis, all of which are involved, will be a very slow process, particularly if the government receives many more applications than it had first anticipated.
It is expected that the first compensation to any UFFI home owner who is seeking a grant will not be made until at least September. This is due to the long process which I have just described. The first payment will be made probably in the early fall, yet when looking at this bill, we see that the funding for it is to terminate in December of this year. Here we have the first payments not being made until the early fall while the money incorporated in the bill runs out in December of 1982.
What does the government intend to do if there is a greater number of UFFI victims who qualify for compensation? Are there any provisions for extending the level of compensation and the time limits so people who have applied will be able to qualify for this very limited payment? Otherwise, will we have to go through the whole legislative process again, such as we are doing now, to compensate additional victims of UFFI who did not have an opportunity to apply for compensation within that very limited and restricted time-frame which the government has placed under the provisions of this bill?
In fact, the bill applies only to a very limited number of UFFI victims in the near future. It only applies to those who realize now that they are victims of urea formaldehyde foam insulation. What about those people who discover they are victims of UFFI and develop health problems in five, ten or fifteen years from now? What provisions is the government making for them? It is very likely that many people will not know immediately that they have health problems because of this insulation. It may not become apparent for some years. Will the government have a legal obligation to pay compensation to these home owners in the future? The minister has not even made mention of these people.
The bill does far too little for far too few UFFI victims. The $5,000 grant will not even remove insulation in homes with serious health hazards. It will not pay for removing that insulation. It will only pay for government inspection and testing, and then, as an attempt to forget the problem, it will pay for the painting and sealing of walls, building double walls and increasing the ventilation as if to somehow paper or plaster over the problem. And then it will walk away from the whole problem to forget it ever existed. Unfortunately, that is not the case.
My colleague asks, "Who will buy these homes?" What about all those other home owners whose homes are filled with
urea formaldehyde foam insulation but who do not suffer any health problems at the present time, nor do they have a level of 0.1 per cent in their homes? What about all of the others who, apart from those two criteria, are UFFI users? Those people simply do not qualify for any compensation under Bill C-109. However, the problem will not go away for them, if a person such as this still has UFFI in his home, thanks to the government's approval of UFFI as an appropriate insulation for his home, he will find that the goverment has completely reneged on its responsibilites to persons such as he and to the thousands of other home owners in this same category.
In my constituency of Kingston and the Islands, there are some 2,000 UFFI victims, 2,000 households where urea formaldehyde foam insulation has been installed. However, they banded together to form a chapter of the UFFI Homeowners Association. They have taken part in rallies and have invited the minister to come. They have made pleas to-
He would not come, Flora.

As my colleague, the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) said, the minister simply would not turn up at these rallies. He never turns up at these rallies. He would rather ignore the whole situation and forget his whole role and his responsibility for shafting these unsuspecting home owners.
Leave them out to dry.

Many of the Kingston home owners, those 2,000 people whom I have mentioned, will not be eligible for compensation under this bill. They are in very serious difficulty. The market value of their homes has significantly dropped. It has significantly dropped because of the fact that they have UFFI in their homes. The real estate agents will not even list their homes for sale.
I want to quote from some of the many letters I have received. I am sure that all my colleagues have received letters like this from people who are suffering because of the program the government foisted on them. Perhaps it is their pleas in their letters which will touch the hearts of those in the government, if such hearts exist. I am not sure, considering that hardhearted group over there, whether anything will touch them, but at least it might touch their pocketbooks and they might do something to provide some relief for those people. For example, consider a letter from a woman who wrote to me not long ago concerning this problem. She stated:
Dear Miss MacDonald,
We bought our first home, a one and a half storey, wood frame house, in November of 1980 and had urea formaldehyde foam insulation installed in December of 1980 under the Canadian Home Improvement Program grant. We had been very happy with the added comfort in our homes, both in summer and winter, and we suffer no health problems. Our son was born in 1981, and he suffers no ill effects either.
However, UFFI does present one serious problem for us-public opinion has made our home unsaleable and has drastically reduced the value of it. All the work we did and all the money that we saved for our home has now been for nothing. My husband, a biomedical electronics technician, had worked in Alberta for five years and accepted a maintenance mechanic job with a friend in
May 10, 1982

Kingston in order to return to Ontario where we were married. There was the understanding that he would return to biomedical electronics. However, we have now lost our mobility and no jobs are available in his field in Kingston.
The situation is very depressing to us. We have to set aside too many of the dreams and the plans that we had for our lives.
We feel that since CHIP supported us in having UFFI installed, we should now be receiving support from them. We need the UFFI removed from our home and our home made saleable to the public, so we can go on with living our lives.
That is one type of letter that I received. Another one came from a gentleman who said:
I am writing to ask you to urge the government to take immediate action to alleviate the intolerable suffering and mental anxiety being experienced by those home owners burdened with urea formaldehyde insulation. For a society that has accepted, and indeed has been conditioned to rely on government regulation of consumer products and services, an immoral situation arises when those agencies shirk the responsibility of their actions and ignore the people affected by them. It is incongruous that these agencies encouraged and assisted these home owners to use this material in the first place.
What now exists is a scenario in which
(a)	hundreds are suffering from the symptoms associated with formaldehyde gas.
(b)	others, while not exhibiting physical symptoms, are haunted by the thoughts of being surrounded by a suspected carcinogen.
(c)	many thousands whose properties are treated as lepers, their homes an albatross about their neck, their savings, their dreams effectively wiped out.
No one in this situation was looking for a bargain-it was a premium-priced
product. Some may even have been motivated by a sense of good citizenship.
From the evidence now available in the scientific literature it is obvious that further testing is unnecessary. I strongly urge that the government divert the millions already committed for testing to a program of restitution for all who are saddled with this unhappy mess. Once effected, some may even want to reaffirm their belief in good citizenship.
Another letter states:
Sir,
This letter is to inform you that the assistance program for UFFI victims, as announced by the federal goverment, is completely unacceptable to me, as I'm sure it must be to all similarly victimized home owners. I must reiterate that my previous claims of government fault in allowing the continued use of UFFI, after NRC warnings to the contrary, are still valid.
This then, necessitates the only honourable solution to this national disaster, complete compensation for the removal of UFFI from all such homes, irrespective of levels of gas-a criterion which has, after all, been proven unrealistic!
I have already informed the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs by telegram of my disgust with, and rejection of, the proposed program. To you .. . and to all ministers to whom this letter is addressed-
This one was addressed to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with a copy to me, and he states:
-I demand that you give the UFFI disaster the full attention it warrants and that the government cease the stalling tactics it has seen fit to practice since early last year when the dangers of this product were finally brought to the attention of the people of this country.
We victims have suffered enough from the complete disregard of human dignity that the federal government has seen Fit to adhere to in this matter! I am sure that a similar circumstance arising in a third world country would have received the instant and full attention of the Canadian government-
In closing, may I say that I remain confident that right will prevail and that you in government will recognize your responsibilities-
I have a final letter, although I could go on with a number of them, which states:
In the summer of 1979, along with many thousands of other home owners, I succumbed to the pleas of the government and insulated the walls of my older home with urea formaldehyde. The contractor did a very satisfactory job. The home uses less fuel, the Queen's University Occupational Health Resources Centre has tested the inside of the house for formaldehyde gas and found no sign.
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
However, I find that if I want to sell it or rent it, it has very little market value. Even the lending institutions don't want to put a mortgage on it. My wife and I have not experienced any ill health that might be attributed to the presence of gas, but it seems that the only course open to us, if we want to dispose of this home in the future, is to have the insulation removed.
I now have a quotation of $4,700 from a reliable contractor and would consider it only fair ball if the government, which considered its CHIP contribution in 1979 as a taxable benefit, would now allow the cost of removal as a tax deductible expense. It seems that we cannot expect any direct compensation in our circumstances. That creep Ouellet-
Those are not my words, but words I am reading.
That creep Ouellet is keeping a very low profile these days and 1 don't suppose you would get very far with this idea, but would appreciate if you would put forward the suggestion for consideration.
These are some of the many letters coming to people like me, members of Parliament, and, I would say, to those on both sides of the House, even if I do not hear complaints being raised by those in the Liberal back benches. However, I imagine there would be many such letters.

speakerposition: Deputy Leader of the Government in the Senate
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wonder whether the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) would entertain a question at this point.

When I am through speaking, Mr. Speaker, I would be delighted to entertain a question from the parliamentary secretary.
These letters show that there are many homes throughout Canada that have lost their value. Therefore, many of the home owners have applied to tax assessors for tax reassessment of their homes. This is going on in every municipality across the country.
All of the UFFI home owners in Kingston have appealed for a reassessment. In light of the recent precedent set in Sault Ste. Marie in which 36 home owners won a 50 per cent reduction in their home tax assessment, the Kingston home owner appeal looks very probably and possible of acceptance.
Is the federal government willing to sit back and watch homes and properties be devalued? It will reflect very considerably on municipal tax revenues. That is the real cause of concern. In the case of Ontario municipalities, it can mean a possible loss of $5 million to $6 million a year. That is what is estimated as a loss in tax revenues in municipalities because of the devaluation of the homes and subsequent tax reassessment.
This issue has been raised persistently in the House. It has been raised over and over again by members of the opposition. The minister has persistently ignored the problem. Can the government not understand that it has a moral duty to the home owners where UFFI has been installed? When it approved the use of UFFI as part of the CHIP program, the responsibility for the CHIP program, the responsibility for the CHIP program and all of its consequences rested squarely on the shoulders of the government. That cannot be ignored.
The cost of complete removal of the foam has been estimated at anywhere from $10,000 to $100,000 per home. Thus, the implications for borrowing money to remove the foam are

May 10, 1982
Urea Formaldehyde Insulation Act
clear. With existing high interest rates, borrowing money to remove UFFI is something that is beyond the consideration of home owners in Canada today.
One letter I received was from a man who was so desperate-and he was describing the situation to another person- that when he considered the situation in which he found himself, "his voice was shaky". Near tears, he told me that his family, particularly his children aged three and one, had been suffering from severe health problems caused by the foam. His wife was working, so with two incomes the family was able to move into an apartment. The health problems stopped immediately. However, his wife will soon lose her job. He will not be able to maintain the house and apartment. He cannot get rid of the house and will not able to afford the apartment in which they live because of health reasons.
What is this man and his family to do? Where do they turn? The least the government could do for all UFFI home owners is to permit them to claim the cost of UFFI as a tax deductible expense.
My colleague, the hon. member for Hamilton-Wentworth (Mr. Scott) has raised this option in question period as an extremely valid and acceptable direction for the minister to take in addressing the problems facing UFFI home owners. The recommendation, like all other questions on the issue of UFFI, was ignored by the minister, and any responsibility for the UFFI mess on the part of the federal government was categorically denied over and over again.
I plead the urgency of the issue, as do UFFI home owners everywhere. Last Saturday 500 members of HUFFI, a group which has banded together to try to do something about this, from across Ontario rallied in Toronto to state their concerns. These home owners are exasperated, confused and desperate. They want something done. They want to be able to remove the insulation now, while the weather is good. That is the reason for their urgency. They do not want to put up with another winter during which UFFI can do more and more damage.
Imagine living in a home, day by day knowing that the fumes or gases from the insulation in the walls is taking its toll on your health and the health of your family. What would you do in a situation like that? Wouldn't you complain? That is all these people are doing. All this concern, both for one's health and one's financial situation, were caused by a major error in judgment on the part of the federal government.
Bill C-109 is simply not acceptable if it is to be the federal government's only response to this serious and widespread UFFI crisis that exists all across Canada.
The president of HUFFI, Frank Spitzer, described the bill as "a mild bandage to help with the fact that you've got a major wound that needs surgery". The issue is not simply one of home owners in trouble needing support from the government. It is a moral issue which the government has the moral responsibility to address. It is as straightforward as that.
A federal agency, CMHC, accepted and approved UFFI as one of a number of alternative insulations which could be
installed in a home owner's house under the CHIP program. The government approved it. If the approval had never been made, none of the thousands of UFFI home owners who took advantage of the CHIP program and consequently do not find themselves in this difficult situation would be in such a bind. If the government had not taken that step in the first place, these people would be free of the problems they are now locked into. They simply would have used one of the other forms of insulation and would be leading a much less troublesome and a much healthier existence.
The reality is that the government did approve UFFI. Therefore, the government cannot ignore its responsibility to compensate, not just a token number of UFFI home owners as Bill C-109 does, but rather all home owners who took the government at its word and believed in the credibility of the program that it was putting forward. For them and for many other Canadians, that credibility has now been shattered.

subtopic: THE ECONOMY-CABINET MEETING AT MEACH LAKE, P.Q.-(B) SITUATION IN CANADA VIS-A-VIS UNITED STATES-(C) GOVERNMENT POSITION
THE ECONOMY-CABINET MEETING AT MEACH LAKE, P.Q.-(B) SITUATION IN CANADA VIS-A-VIS UNITED STATES-(C) GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 27 I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) about the Meach lake conference, where members of the cabinet met together and enjoyed themselves for a weekend and came out with absolutely nothing to solve the economic problems of the country. A day after the cabinet meeting the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism (Mr. Lapointe) was caught by a reporter in the province of Quebec, and he said:
We are fearful that if there is a recovery in the United States we would not be able to join the band wagon.
It appears to be the view of the government that we will not be able to get out of the depression the minister and his colleagues have caused.
The three questions I asked on April 27 were about the Meach Lake conference, where it became clear to the government that it is totally out of touch with the realities of the country. The members of the cabinet came out of that conference, and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) said, "We are going to carry on in the same way". The minister responsible for lotteries said, "We are going to carry on in the same way", and the next day the Minister of State for Small Businesses and Tourism said, "There is no way we can get out of this. Even if the United States recovers, we are down the poop-chute anyway."	.
I want to comment tonight on that very problem because the truth of the matter, as Mr. Mulholland of the Bank of Montreal has said, is that this government has developed an attitude of pessimism. It has developed the attitude that there will be a lack of growth. It has developed an attitude of anti-investment, anti-entrepreneurialism and anti-growth. In this country there is a negative outlook, to the extent that a survey undertaken by the Toronto Star showed that 60 per cent of businessmen surveyed felt that profits would be down, 75 per cent of businessmen interviewed said that this is not a time to invest and 55 per cent of businessmen interviewed said that the Canadian dollar would depreciate in value.
Because of the attitude of this government shown in its budget and national energy policy, because of its attitude toward foreign investment and, indeed, because of its attitude
Adjournment Debate
toward Canadian investment the government has engendered in the community a fear that no matter what happens, even if there is recovery in the United States, we will not have recovery here.
I was in the United States at the Easter weekend. There seems to be optimism there respecting growth and the future. There seems to be feeling that there will be a better tomorrow and that now is the time to make deals. When a recovery occurs in the United States, as it surely will-there is now a zero rate of inflation-money will flee from Canada to the United States to take advantage of the real opportunities which will be there. We will wind up not being able to take advantage of opportunities and still in the doldrums with more and more people out of work, without hope and without opportunity. That is what we have been left with-that is the legacy of a government that really does not care.
That government went to Meach Lake and enjoyed the sunshine of early spring in the Gatineau hills. What it did there we do not know. It may have had some economic discussions, but the minister would not say that. It came away from Meach Lake with nothing at all to offer. That is what it gives the people of Canada; no hope, no future, no possibilities. The ministry has to answer, Mr. Speaker.

speakeroldname: Mr. Gary F. McCauley (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: THE ECONOMY-CABINET MEETING AT MEACH LAKE, P.Q.-(B) SITUATION IN CANADA VIS-A-VIS UNITED STATES-(C) GOVERNMENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is wondering about the capacity of the Canadian economy to respond to any recovery in the United States. There is no doubt in my mind that a recovery in the United States will have a favourable impact on the Canadian economy. At the moment, the weakness in U.S. demand is, not surprisingly, restricting our export opportunities. But when growth in the U.S. resumes within the next few months, export growth will contribute to the recovery in Canada. To the extent that the U.S. recovery will be accompanied by lower interest rates, this will mean lower interest rates in Canada as well; this will provide stimulus to our interest-sensitive sectors.
What is uncertain, and this might be what the hon. member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) was trying to say, is the ability of Canada to get the most out of any U.S. recovery that would take place. As my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) keeps pointing out, there is a danger that Canadians will price themselves out of world markets unless a sustained effort is made to reduce inflation.
The United States has made remarkable progress against inflation lately but we in Canada have made much less progress. In March, the year-over-year increase in the U.S. consumer price index was 6.7 per cent, whereas the corresponding rate in Canada was 11.6 per cent. It is important that the government stick to its non-accommodating fiscal and monetary policies, thereby reducing inflation and preserving our competitiveness in external markets.

May 10, 1982
Adjournment Debate
Let me now turn to the hon. member's mention of an overpriced Canadian dollar. Does he realize that a lower value for the Canadian dollar means higher import costs for Canadian producers and higher import prices for Canadian consumers? This would result in significant upward pressures on our inflation rate. Of course a lower Canadian dollar would tend to improve our competitive position and encourage our exports. But the gain in our competitive position produced by the depreciation would be eroded quickly owing to the renewed impetus given to inflation by higher import prices.

subtopic: CORPORATE AFFAIRS-INVESTIGATION OF CONSOLIDATED COMPUTERS INC. (B) ROLE OF ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
CORPORATE AFFAIRS-INVESTIGATION OF CONSOLIDATED COMPUTERS INC. (B) ROLE OF ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over a month ago, on March 29, I asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) about the collapse of Consolidated Computers Inc. which cost Canadian taxpayers well over $100 million. A report from Treasury Board, the so-called Anderson report, on this debacle characterized its findings with words such as conflict of interest, incompetence and cover-up. I hoped that the minister would reassure me at that time that the commercial crime section of the RCMP was well on its way to an investigation of the whole scenario. Instead, the minister merely indicated "that a reference was made to the Department of Justice under the section of the relevant statute requiring the minister to see that the administration of the public sector is in accordance with the law".
The time has come once more, after all these weeks, vigorously to bring to the attention of the House and the government that enough time has elapsed so that the Canadian people should be informed precisely what happened to the government investigation, who was responsible for this debacle and who benefited from this vast amount of money that has obviously been squandered and frittered away.
Personally, Sir, I have reason to believe that more than just incompetence and bureaucratic duplicity are involved here. I am convinced what we have here is an example of rotten pork-barrel politics, and it is time for a full accounting. We know, thanks to the Anderson report from the Treasury Board, that the company had little or nothing in the way of meaningful controls, so much so that the respected accounting firm of Thorne Riddell, after discussions with Miss Dale Robinette of the firm of McCarthy and McCarthy, a respected Toronto law firm, would not accept the responsibility of making decisions on which leases would be purchased from Consolidated Computer. Instead, they preferred only, in the words of the Anderson report, to be administrators of the leased companies for which, incidentally, they received over $100,000 a year.
The Anderson report cites many examples of poor management and potential conflicts of interest. The chief executive officer of CCI, John McDonald Brown, the man touted so highly by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray) in his letter of June 3, 1980, to the President of the
Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) is noted as having retained his membership on the Enterprise Development Board while he was chairman and chief executive officer of this wretched company, CCI. While the company completed its disintegration under Mr. Brown's leadership, he submitted a formal application on his own behalf and that of some associates to purchase some shares in the company. The Anderson report goes on to point out that he was simultaneously a member of the Enterprise Development Board which controlled the shares being offered for sale, the chairman and president of the company whose shares were up for sale, and an applicant to purchase the shares. The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce touted Mr. Brown as a saviour of this company. Well, if he was a saviour, I would hate to see what he would have done had he intended to do any harm, since about $30 million went down the drain under his stewardship in a very short time.
For this Mr. Brown was paid quite well with a contract for $110,000 per year, payable quarterly in advance, and other perks. H. J. Melanson, executive vice-president, was plugged in firmly, too, at $500 a week overtime, effective July 1, 1981, to supplement his annual salary of $49,000. And so the story goes.
Surely the minister will soon call for a proper inquiry under the Inquiries Act to look in a comprehensive way at the sorry affair. But one might well ask tonight: who is this John McDonald Brown? What were his real qualifications? Who are his associates? Did Mr. Brown became a computer expert because of his association with Mr. Gordon Hughes? It is interesting to note that Gordon Hughes is a close friend and confidante of the then premier of Nova Scotia, and he has numerous corporate interests in the province. He is also a director of the CRTC, a close friend of Senator Irvine Barrow, and a director of the CTC. Or did Mr. Brown pick up his expertise from Mr. Green? Here we have a situation where it might not be a tale of patronage in black and white, Mr. Speaker, but it may be one of Brown and Green. Mr. Green is a prominent barrister in the law firm of Kitz, Matheson, Green and Maclsaac in Nova Scotia, commonly known as "Kitz, Matheson, Green and patronage" by people who study the political scene. He is a prominent Liberal, a former executive legislative counsel to the Secretary of State (Mr. Regan) when he was premier of Nova Scotia, a former campaign manager and adviser, as well as former co-chairman of the leadership campaign of the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) for the Liberal Party in 1968, and federal campaign chairman for the Liberals in the federal elections of 1968 and 1972. Or did Mr. McDonald Brown get this expertise by virtue of work done by himself and his associates towards the electoral success of the Minister of Finance? In any case, Sir, Brown, Green and Hughes, and others I could name, are all close business and political associates, all prominent Liberals and have all participated in one way or another in numerous soft loans and other advantageous deals in Nova Scotia. The question is now, have they moved on

to the national scene, perhaps through the ill-fated Consolidated Computers Incorporated?

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay) has indicated, he asked the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chretien) on March 29 about information regarding an investigation of Consolidated Computer. The Department of Justice has been requested by the Treasury Board to review the report entitled "Report Concerning Involvement of Government of Canada in Affairs of CCI" from the standpoint of its legal implications. The hon. member wanted to know if it was a departmental inquiry under the Inquiries Act.
This examination, he should know, is being conducted, pursuant to Section 4 of the Department of Justice Act which makes it mandatory for the minister to, "see that the administration of public affairs is in accordance with law" and not under the Inquiries Act, as suggested.
The task which the Department of Justice has before it is large and complex. The report and the background material will require a detailed study. It is difficult to assess the length of time such a detailed study would take. However, the urgency of the matter is appreciated. I may add, however, that if a need for further investigation is indicated this will be done.
