subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REPORTED CANADA-FRANCE AGREEMENT ON SAINT PIERRE AND MIQUELON ISLANDS. (B) REQUEST THAT AGREEMENT BE MADE PUBLIC

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REPORTED CANADA-FRANCE AGREEMENT ON SAINT PIERRE AND MIQUELON ISLANDS. (B) REQUEST THAT AGREEMENT BE MADE PUBLIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 27 I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) a question about the dispute between Canada and France over the problem of the boundaries between those two countries surrounding Saint Pierre and Miquelon. The minister showed an amazing lack of knowledge about this very serious matter, serious because it affects a huge area of the continental shelf and the possible gas, oil and other minerals under that continental shelf, and because it affects fishing areas jointly claimed by both countries.
In responding to my question, the minister said he was not aware of an agreement which the government had signed in 1972. As a matter of fact, it was signed on May 26, 1972, in Paris. This agreement was signed by the representative for Canada, Mr. Alan Beasley, head of the Canadian delegation, and by the head of the French delegation. The document was headed "releve de conclusions". Linder the terms of that document, this government blundered tremendously.
This is the reason, in my view, why ten years later we still have no answer or settlement of the boundary dispute between these two countries. The matter has not gone to arbitration because the Canadian government botched so badly ten years ago when that document was originally signed by the ambassador on behalf of the Canadian government. What did that agreement do? What it did was to give France, through Saint Pierre and Miquelon, rights and special privileges in an area of 22,000 square miles of the continental shelf off the south coast of Newfoundland. On about half of that area Canada was to be required to give oil companies designated by France exclusive rights and on the other half the Canadian government was to recommend that its permitees in that area would have to form joint ventures-Mobil and Gulf were involved-that would have to give French companies substantial rights. In the case of both of these areas the government of France would be able to remove oil and gas found through Saint Pierre. In return, France was to renounce formal legal claims to the area and would get sovereignty over a 12-mile territorial limit around Saint Pierre and Miquelon.
Saint Pierre and Miquelon are two very small islands. Saint Pierre is ten square miles and Miquelon is 83 square miles. Miquelon has a population of 500. The total population for both islands is 5,800. Those islands are only 15 miles off the mouth of Fortune Bay in Newfoundland.
Canada owns an island called Little Green Island only three miles away from Saint Pierre and Miquelon. It can hardly be serious that anyone should think France would have a claim for 22,000 square miles or do anything like that under international law.
The minister also went ahead on April 27 to say that negotiations had not been going on for 11 years on these issues but that they had only commenced in 1976. This was the same

May 10, 1982
Adjournment Debate
minister who had just met with the French prime minister several days earlier to discuss this issue. How could he properly represent Canada when he apparently did not know that these negotiations started not in 1976 but in 1966?
I have here an answer which was made by the French minister of foreign affairs in the National Assembly of France on October 29, 1975 when he said:
Negotiations were begun in 1966 between France and Canada with the view of delimiting the continental shelf of the two states in the area of the islands of Saint Pierre and Miquelon.
Then he went on to describe how the French were claiming that the "principle of equidistance" applied and that Canada invoked the principle of "special circumstances" to reduce the French claim. Then he went on to say:
-at a meeting held in Paris on 26 May 1972 the heads of the delegations signed a "releve de conclusions"-
He was referring to an agreement to deal with this matter. Also he said:
Despite France's repeated requests, the Canadian government has never approved this document ... On his visit to Paris in autumn 1974, Mr. Trudeau told the Prime Minister that he would make efforts to bring about the settlement of the matter.
Of course he was referring to the French prime minister. This is a matter where negotiations, according to the minister, did not start until 1976. The minister, in his answer to me, said that he was unaware that an agreement was ever signed.
The agreement has been embarrassing the Canadian government ever since. It was a blunder. It was stopped. The Canadian government was stopped from ratifying it by the government of Newfoundland and Labrador. The new Conservative administration which had been elected in January 1972 had started inquiring as to what was happening with reference to this boundary dispute. When that government started inquiring, the Canadian government realized that it had made a blunder and never ratified the agreement signed by its ambassador. It has been an embarrassment to Canada ever since.
Back in March 1971 the then Canadian secretary of state for external affairs said that the Canadian argument was that special circumstances justified another boundary. Then he went on to indicate that if a settlement satisfactory to Canada could not be reached on the basis of negotiation, the government would be prepared to refer the matter for arbitration. It was 11 years ago that the then secretary of state for external affairs said that if a settlement satisfactory to us could not be reached on the negotiation, the government would refer it to arbitration. There have been 11 years of known negotiations, and the time has long since gone for this to be referred to arbitration. The only possible reason there might be for not referring the issue to arbitration is the damage done by this administration by having this agreement signed in May 1972.
This is an important matter. About a month ago French authorities in Saint Pierre and Miquelon made a request of Paris to send out a gun boat because the Canadian government was inspecting certain French fishing trawlers. Canadian fishing trawlers had been stopped by France. On November 24, 1981, officials from the French vessel Tenace boarded two Canadian fishing vessels and searched them in the disputed
area. What is Canada to do if France sends out a gun boat? We all know that our navy is not in shape to even defend us from a gun boat. If we were in the position of Argentina and we were to occupy these islands, we would have to row across the 13 miles from the mouth of Fortune Bay over to Saint Pierre and Miquelon. I just cite this example to show that it is a very serious matter over which there can be trouble in the future if it is not settled.
How can the government protect our interests if the government does not even have a Secretary of State for External Affairs who knows the most rudimentary points about the history of the situation, who appears to be unconcerned, who is not negotiating now to have the matter settled, who is not prepared to refer this to arbitration, and when we have a Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) who exhibits utter indifference? He met with Mr. Mitterrand several times in the last 12 months. He met with the Prime Minister of France in the last 12 months. Yet nothing continues to happen with reference to this situation.
I also point out that in a case which went to the International Court of Justice and arbitration in 1979 between the U.K. and France concerning the delimitation of the continental shelf, the International Court of Justice accepted the agreement of May 26, 1972, which I mentioned earlier, as an agreement between Canada and France on the continental shelf. That will show you the damage that has been done to us by that agreement.
Therefore, when will this matter be pressed to a solution? Will the government publish this agreement? Will the government give us the details of what the French are claiming, and will this matter go to arbitration this year and not be allowed to be delayed another 11 years?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS-REPORTED CANADA-FRANCE AGREEMENT ON SAINT PIERRE AND MIQUELON ISLANDS. (B) REQUEST THAT AGREEMENT BE MADE PUBLIC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in 1972 Canada and France signed a fisheries agreement which included a provision delimiting the territorial sea and fishing zone between Saint Pierre and Miquelon and Newfoundland, that is the area landward of the French islands. In that same year a "releve de conclusions", or a summary of conclusions, was signed at the level of officials dealing with the continental shelf seaward of Saint Pierre and Miquelon. This latter document specifically stated that the agreed conclusions would be submitted to the two governments for approval. Thus the releve was not an agreement or even an agreement ad referendum since, had it been approved by governments, another document constituting a formal agreement would have had to be drafted. Indeed, the releve itself expressly foresaw the need for a bilateral agreement of the delimitation of the continental shelf in the event neither government ever approved the releve.
In late 1977 it came to our attention that the releve had been referred to in the pleadings and in the decision of the Ad Hoc Court of Arbitration in the Anglo-French Channel islands
May 10, 1982

case. In a diplomatic note to France, Canada noted the Arbitration Court's reference to the releve as an agreement, and indicated that in the absence of the requisite governmental approval the document clearly did not constitute any such agreement. In response, the French acknowledged that the releve, "may not be considered as an agreement, even of a provisional nature" as it never had been approved by either side.
Following Canadian and French extension of jurisdiction of 200 miles in 1977, Canada and France undertook to proceed with negotiations on the delimitation of the area seaward of Saint Pierre and Miquelon. Several rounds of negotiations
Adjournment Debate
have taken place since then. This matter was most recently raised by both Prime Minister Mauroy and Foreign Minister Cheysson during their April visit to Ottawa, and the two sides agreed on the need actively to pursue efforts to delineate this disputed maritime boundary.
